CLASS 37 · AGES 4–5 · 40 MOVEMENT LESSONS

Sports, Movement & Play.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Forty sports, forty big moves, one active playground.

Every sport in this class is taught as ONE big move your child can try today: the soccer plant-and-swing, the basketball push-and-catch, the frog-jump landing, the pencil dive, the egg-beater float. Each card comes with its step-by-step lesson right here — what the sport is, the three ideas your child needs, the parent script, one game for the living room and, where it matters, the safety rule said out loud. The order is deliberate: the ball games a four-year-old already knows come first, then run-jump-throw athletics, the water sports, wheels and boards and ice, climbing and riding, aim and precision, the martial arts, and the mighty lift at the end.

One card a sitting is plenty — the whole class is a term of five-minute active visits. The vocabulary is the one early-years teachers use: gross motor skills, physical literacy and the fundamental movement skills — run, jump, throw, catch, kick, balance — the same words New Zealand and Australian schools teach as the heart of movement, and Canadian families know as the path to physical literacy. By the end, your child has forty named skills and forty games that grow them.

WHY MOVEMENT MATTERS

The body learns first.

Before pencils and letters come legs and lungs: active play builds the balance, grip and coordination that every classroom skill quietly borrows. This class does not train champions — it hands your child the movement words (jump, throw, glide, balance, kick) and the joy of using them, so that whatever sport your family meets next — school sports day, a swim class, a dance group — the door is already open.

And the safety rules live inside the lessons where they belong: helmets before wheels, grown-ups before water, pads before wheels roll and mats before falls. Every rule is said out loud in its lesson, every time — that repetition is the lesson.

Forty movement cards, one picture each. Every lesson is right here on this page — the original artwork beside the step-by-step teaching: what the sport is, the three ideas your child needs, the script to say and one game to play tonight.

Soccer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches soccer the way four-year-olds actually meet it: foot meets ball, ball goes somewhere, and the somewhere gets steered — one gentle step at a time.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Soccer is a team game played with one ball and mostly feet: kick it to a friend, dribble it down the field, and kick it into the net to score. Only the goalkeepers may use hands.

What does it mean?

For a small child soccer is the first sport where a tool is replaced by a body part: the foot must do what a hand would do — aim, carry, stop. That switch-on is why soccer is the world’s first sport for four-year-olds in almost every country.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three soccer ideas: the kick is a swing from the hip with the toe down; the OTHER foot plants beside the ball like a anchor; and the freeze-stop — one sole on top of the ball — is how players own the ball instead of chasing it.

Why this matters

Soccer opens this class because it is the most universal gross motor activity on the wall: a ball, a patch of ground, done. It is also the friendliest miss in sport — a ball that rolls away simply waits to be kicked again.

What it teaches

Kicking (the last of the big ball skills to mature), single-leg balance on the plant foot, steering a rolling object with taps — the dribble — plus turn-taking in the goal game.

Words to learn

soccerkickgoaldribblestopfieldteam

Say this to your child

“"Soccer is kicking the ball with your feet — hands stay home! Plant your strong foot next to the ball like a tree, swing the other one, toe down… and there it goes. And when the ball tries to run away? You put your foot on top and say FREEZE. The ball stops. The ball is yours."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is soccer — the game where feet do everything."
  2. Demo the kick slowly: plant foot beside the ball, swing the kicking leg from the hip, toe down, contact. Make the plant foot the star — "this foot stands still like a tree."
  3. Teach the freeze-stop: roll the ball gently, your child runs it down and puts one sole on top — freeze! Practise three rolls.
  4. First dribble: kick, walk, kick, walk — the ball stays a pet on a leash, never running away.
  5. Finish with the chair-goal game below and the takeaway sentence: "I kick, I stop, the ball is mine."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "soccer" sits in big letters at the top, with the game’s own scene below — the sport exactly as your child will meet it on the field, one ball, big grass.

Ask your child

"What do we kick the ball with in soccer?" "Can we pick it up?" "How do we stop the ball when it runs away?" "Where does a goal go in?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "You kick it with your feet!" "No hands!" or the proud one: "I froze the ball — it stopped!"

Out in the real world

Any grass, any hallway, any ball. Point out soccer everywhere it lives: the park game on Sunday, the World Cup on the screen, the neighbour’s kid dribbling past the fence. One real "I kick like that too!" is worth ten drills.

Try it together

Freeze-the-Ball: you roll the ball gently across the room, your child chases it down and freezes it with one foot on top. Then swap — you freeze, they roll. Three freezes each, then the chair-goal opens and every freeze earns one shot. Roll, chase, freeze, shoot — the whole first soccer class, played.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which foot plants like a tree? What do we say when the foot lands on the ball? How many hands does a goalkeeper get?" Plant foot, freeze, two — three answers and the first lesson of the class is won.

Parent tips

If the kick keeps missing, shrink the ball, not the child: a size-1 mini ball or even a soft toy is easier to steer and builds the same swing. And never rush the hands rule — goalkeepers get hands, and today your child can BE the goalkeeper for one round, diving on the ball with both hands like the pros.

This lesson pairs with the Soccer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Basketball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches basketball from the palm down: the ball lives on the floor, comes back up by itself, and every bounce is a conversation between hand and ball.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Basketball is a team game with a bouncing ball and two raised hoops: dribble by bouncing, pass by throwing, score by dropping the ball through the hoop.

What does it mean?

Basketball is the only major sport where the ball asks to come back — bounce it and it returns to your hand. For a child that return is irresistible: it makes ten repetitions feel like ten turns of a game, which is exactly how throwing skills get their reps.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three basketball ideas: the bounce is a PUSH, not a slap — fingers spread, ball pressed down; the catch is soft hands that pull the ball in like a hug; and a shot is an arc — up and over, not at the hoop.

Why this matters

Of every card on this wall, basketball grows hand-eye coordination fastest, because bounce-and-catch repeats in seconds. It also teaches the vertical game — up, over, down — that volleyball and tennis will borrow later.

What it teaches

Object control (push-catch), hand-eye timing, arc awareness for aiming at raised targets, and the two-hand pattern that underpins every catch in sport.

Words to learn

basketballbouncedribblecatchhooparcshot

Say this to your child

“"Basketball is the bouncing game! Push the ball down with your starfish hand — and look, it comes back up to say hello. Catch it soft, like a hug. And when we shoot, we shoot a rainbow — up, up, over, and… swish!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is basketball — the bouncing game."
  2. Hand out the bounce: fingers spread like a starfish, push the ball down at your side. It comes back — that is the magic. Five pushes.
  3. Teach the soft catch: arms out, fingers wide, pull the ball IN as it arrives — hugging hands, not fence posts. Ten gentle tosses.
  4. Show the arc: shots go UP and over, like a rainbow into the basket. Fire straight and the rim says no.
  5. Play the basket game below and close with: "push down, catch soft, shoot rainbows."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "basketball" stands big at the top with the game’s scene underneath — the bouncing ball and the hoop exactly as your child will meet them on court.

Ask your child

"What does the ball do when we push it down?" "Do we catch it hard or soft?" "Does a shot go straight, or up like a rainbow?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It comes back by itself!" "I caught it soft!" or the shot report: "My rainbow went in — swish!"

Out in the real world

Hoops are everywhere once you look: the park court, the school yard, the mini hoop on a bedroom door. Watch a minute of a real game and find the rainbow shots together — arcs, arcs everywhere.

Try it together

Laundry-Basket Hoop: basket on the floor first — bounce five, then drop-toss it in. Round two: basket on a chair — now the rainbow matters. Round three: basket moves, shooter moves. Every make is a swish-shout, every miss is "one more rainbow." The basket never laughs at a miss, and neither do we.

Understanding check

Ask: "Push or slap? Catch hard or soft? Straight or rainbow?" Push, soft, rainbow — three answers and the ball talks to your child now.

Parent tips

If the bounce keeps escaping, make the hand quieter: push, do not slap, and start the bounce at knee height, not shoulder. And let the ball be silly sometimes — one bounce on the HEAD is worth ten drills for keeping the fun alive.

This lesson pairs with the Basketball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Volleyball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches volleyball’s one big rule first — the ball never touches the floor — and lets the bump grow out of saving it.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Volleyball is a net game between two teams: bump, set or spike the ball over, and never let it land on your side. Three touches is the grown-up limit; one glorious bump is the four-year-old limit.

What does it mean?

Volleyball is the only sport on this wall where the ground is the enemy. That single rule makes children lift their eyes off the floor and into the air — a whole new ball-sport posture, and the reason volleyball players read the sky.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three volleyball ideas: the bump is FLAT forearms joined like a shelf, not hands; the ball is met, not hit — legs push up as the ball lands on the shelf; and the team shout "mine!" is part of the skill.

Why this matters

The bump is the gentlest contact skill in sport — no grip, no swing, just a shelf that helps the ball up. It is the perfect first team sport for children who find hitting a ball hard but love keeping things alive.

What it teaches

Underarm contact control, reading a falling object, the joined-forearm platform, and calling "mine!" — the first team-communication skill on the whole wall.

Words to learn

volleyballbumpnetrallykeep it upmineteam

Say this to your child

“"Volleyball is the no-drop game! We make a shelf with our arms — flat and strong — and when the ball floats down, our legs lift it back up. Bump! We never let it touch the floor. And we always shout MINE before we bump — that is how teams talk."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is volleyball — the no-drop game."
  2. Build the shelf: arms straight down, forearms together, flat as a table. Ball rests on the shelf — hold it there three seconds.
  3. Teach the meet: when the ball comes down, do not swing — legs push, shelf lifts, ball floats up. Like bouncing it off a trampoline you wear.
  4. Count together: one bump, catch, two bumps, catch — bumps grow one at a time.
  5. Play balloon-volleyball below and end on the team word: "mine!" before every touch.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "volleyball" is printed big at the top, the game’s scene below it — the floating ball over the net exactly as the sport looks from the sand or the court.

Ask your child

"What do we never let the ball touch?" "Do we hit it with fists or meet it with a flat shelf?" "What do we shout before we bump?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The floor is out!" "I made a shelf!" or the proud count: "Three bumps — no drops!"

Out in the real world

Volleyball lives at beaches, backyards and school gyms — and its cousin lives in every living room: balloons. Watch a rally point together and hunt for the bump: flat arms, ball up, team shouting.

Try it together

Balloon Keep-It-Up: a balloon over a string or sofa-cushion net. One bump at a time, catch between rounds, count every bump out loud. When singles get steady, join hands-family-style and bump as a two-person team — "MINE!" before every touch. The balloon hangs long enough for the shelf to find it, and the no-drop rule does the coaching.

Understanding check

Ask: "What must never touch the floor? What do our arms make? What do we shout?" Floor, a shelf, MINE — three answers and the rally is on.

Parent tips

If hands keep sneaking up, tape a soft bracelet on the wrists as a reminder: the bump lives below the bracelet. And let the balloon win sometimes — a chaotic, giggling, everyone-diving rally is the sport’s best advertisement.

This lesson pairs with the Volleyball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Tennis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches tennis as one delicious trick: keep the ball in the air with a thing on the end of your arm — the rally grows out of that trick like a plant.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Tennis is a net game played with rackets: hit the ball over the net, your partner hits it back, and the rally keeps going as long as nobody misses.

What does it mean?

Tennis is the first sport on the wall where the hand plays through a tool. The racket adds reach but subtracts direct touch — the brain must remap hitting, and once it does, every striking sport gets easier.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tennis ideas: the racket face is a flat palm held out in front; the ball is TAPPED, not smashed — a high-five through the ball; and rallies are counting games, not winning games.

Why this matters

Tennis earns an early card because striking is one of the big fundamental movement skills and the balloon-first version needs no court, no net and no strength — just a floating thing worth chasing.

What it teaches

Striking with an implement, tracking a moving object through the air, side-on body position, and the patience of a rally that counts instead of competes.

Words to learn

tennisrackettapnetrallyovercount

Say this to your child

“"Tennis is the tap-it-over game! Your racket is a flat palm on a stick — tap the balloon UP, let it float, tap again. How many taps can we do? Then we turn our body side-on like a real player and tap it over the sofa-net to me. Ping! My turn. Ping! Your turn."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is tennis — the tap-it-over game."
  2. Make the palm-racket connection: hold your flat hand up — that IS the racket face. Now the racket holds the same palm for you.
  3. Tap-up drill: drop the balloon, tap it up with the flat face, let it fall, tap again. Count the taps together — every record is a party.
  4. Turn sideways: feet point at the wall, belly not the net — the sideways stand of every real rally.
  5. Play sofa-net rallies below and close: "flat palm, little tap, over it goes."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "tennis" leads at the top with the game’s scene under it — the racket, the ball and the net exactly as the rally looks from the court.

Ask your child

"What does the racket face look like?" "Do we smash or tap?" "What do we count in a rally?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My racket is a big flat hand!" "I tapped it seven times!" or the rally shout: "Ping — your turn!"

Out in the real world

Tennis lives at parks, clubs and TVs — and its tiny cousins live in every kitchen: a spoon and a pom-pom, a paddle and a balloon. Watch one rally together and hunt for the tap.

Try it together

Sofa-Net Rally: the sofa back is the net, the balloon is the ball. Stand two cushions apart, tap it over, partner taps it back. Balloon rallies last long enough to feel REAL — and when a rally reaches five, the whole room loses its mind. That is the moment tennis hooks a child for good.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the racket face? Tap or smash? What does a rally count?" Flat palm, tap, taps — three answers and the rally has begun.

Parent tips

If the racket scares the game away, play hand-tennis first — the tap is the same skill without the tool. And pick the lightest racket sold: junior foam rackets are toys that happen to be real.

This lesson pairs with the Tennis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Badminton — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches badminton around its kindest gift: the shuttlecock floats, drifts and waits — the slowest ball in sport, and the best teacher of watching eyes.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Badminton is a net game with rackets and a shuttlecock — a feathered cone that flies far and falls slow. Tap it over, and it hangs in the air like a parachute before drifting down.

What does it mean?

Every ball sport asks young eyes to track something fast. Badminton does the opposite: the shuttle floats long enough for the eyes to lead, the feet to arrive and the tap to happen on purpose. It is tracking practice wearing a game.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three badminton ideas: the grip is a friendly handshake on the handle, not a squeeze; the tap is underarm, soft and up; and the shuttle’s wobble is normal — it drifts, and drifting is its charm.

Why this matters

For children who find balls too quick, badminton is the door into racket sports: the slow float buys confidence first, skill second. Many future tennis players discover their swing right here.

What it teaches

Object tracking with generous air time, underarm striking with an implement, patience between hits, and the soft-force lesson — gentler tap, prettier float.

Words to learn

badmintonshuttlecocktapfloatdriftnetgentle

Say this to your child

“"Badminton’s ball is a shuttlecock — a little feather rocket that flies fast then floats down slow as a leaf. We hold the racket like a handshake, tap it softly underneath, and watch it drift. The float is the game: your eyes just follow it, and tap again when it says hello."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is badminton — the game with the feather rocket."
  2. Meet the shuttle: hold it up, drop it, watch it wobble down. "See how it floats? That is why this game is slow and lovely."
  3. Handshake grip: hold the racket like shaking hands with it — thumb wrap friendly, not knuckle-white.
  4. Tap-up drill: underarm taps, shuttle floats up, drifts down, tap again. Count the taps in a whisper — this is the quiet game.
  5. Play the drifting rally below and close: "soft tap, slow float, easy eyes."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "badminton" sits big at the top with the game’s scene below — rackets and the floating shuttle exactly as the slow rally looks on court.

Ask your child

"What is the ball of badminton called?" "Does the shuttle zoom or float?" "How do we hold the racket — like a hammer or a handshake?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It floats like a parachute!" "I tapped it and it drifted!" or the handshake report: "My grip is friendly, not squishy!"

Out in the real world

Badminton lives in gyms, gardens and family picnics — one net and two cheap rackets anywhere. Watch a rally together and point out the drift: the shuttle never falls straight, it wanders down like a leaf.

Try it together

Drift Rally: tap the shuttle over a string-net to a partner, no hurry, no score — just how long can the rally float? Add the Whisper Rule: this game is played quiet. The gentleness is the skill, and the quietness makes it land.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we call the feather ball? Does it fall fast or float? How does the racket say hello?" Shuttlecock, float, handshake — three answers and the quiet game begins.

Parent tips

If the shuttle’s wobble makes taps miss, use a sponge ball first and reintroduce the shuttle as "the fancy one." And play into open space, not over a tight net — drifting is the joy; scoring can wait a year.

This lesson pairs with the Badminton flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Table Tennis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches table tennis as tennis’s small, quick cousin: everything arrives sooner, everything is within one arm’s reach, and the rally fits on a kitchen table.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Table tennis (ping pong) is a net game on a table: small paddles, a light white ball that bounces once on each side, rallies that go ping-pong-ping.

What does it mean?

Table tennis is the rally sport at walking speed for the body and hummingbird speed for the eyes. Because the court is one table, every miss is retrieved in one step — the game never breaks its own rhythm, and rhythm is what it teaches.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three table-tennis ideas: the paddle waits flat like a little wall; the ball is tapped UP first — bounce it on your own side before it crosses; and the eyes lead the hands — watch the ball, the paddle follows.

Why this matters

For small hands and short arms the table is the perfect court: nothing is far, nothing is heavy, and the quick little bounces train the fastest tracking on this whole wall without a single sprint.

What it teaches

Short-range tracking, implement striking with quick timing, the bounce-tap-bounce pattern, and focused watching — eyes on the ball is a trainable muscle.

Words to learn

table tennisping pongpaddlebouncenetrallyquick

Say this to your child

“"Table tennis is ping pong! The paddle waits flat like a little wall. Tap the ball up — bounce — tap again. Then on the table: one bounce on your side, tap it over the book-net to me. Ping! Back it comes. Pong! Quick little eyes, quick little taps."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is table tennis — ping pong! The tiny fast game."
  2. Wall-waiting paddle: hold it flat in front, ball dropped ON it — how long can the ball rest? That flatness is the ready position.
  3. Bounce drill: tap the ball up, let it bounce on the paddle, tap again. Small taps, big counting.
  4. Table rules: your side first, then over the book-net — bounce, tap, over. Ping! Pong!
  5. Play the kitchen rally below and close: "flat paddle, quick eyes, ping pong."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "table tennis" are printed large at the top with the game’s scene beneath — paddles, the small white ball and the low net exactly as the rally looks across the table.

Ask your child

"How big is the court in ping pong?" "What does the paddle do while it waits?" "What do we watch — the ball or the paddle?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The whole game is on the table!" "My paddle is a wall!" or the count: "Ping, pong, ping — I kept it going!"

Out in the real world

Ping pong lives in community halls, holiday parks and grandma’s garage — the world’s most findable sport. Watch one rally together and listen for the sound the game is named after.

Try it together

Kitchen Rally: books down the table-middle as the net, sponge ball for the first rounds. Serve by bounce-tap-over, return by watch-tap-over. Every five returns, both players shout PING PONG and wiggle. The table keeps every ball close enough to try again — rhythm first, points never.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where is the court? What does the paddle look like while it waits? What do we watch?" The table, a flat wall, the ball — three answers and the quick game is on.

Parent tips

A sponge or light plastic ball saves the china and the nerves for the first weeks. And let the serve bounce twice if it wants — the rules can shrink to fit the players; the rally is the prize.

This lesson pairs with the Table Tennis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

Baseball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches baseball in its three beats — swing, run, catch — and lets the diamond grow out of cushions on the living-room floor.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Baseball is a bat-and-glove game on a diamond: hit the ball the pitcher throws, run the four bases, and come home to score. The fielders catch it and throw it back before you get there.

What does it mean?

Baseball is the turn-taking sport: one batter, everyone watching, everyone’s turn comes around. For four-year-olds the diamond also draws the first map of sport — bases are places, home is where the points live.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three baseball ideas: the swing is LEVEL — a door swinging, not an axe falling; the batter stands side-on like a surfer watching the wave; and running the bases is a lap with stops — touch white, run to white.

Why this matters

Off a tee, batting is the most satisfying strike in junior sport: the ball stands still, the swing is fully yours, and the CRACK is instant applause. Every rep rewards itself.

What it teaches

Level swinging with an implement, side-on stance, over-arm throwing to a target, and sequencing — hit, drop the bat, RUN.

Words to learn

baseballbatteeswingbaserunhome

Say this to your child

“"Baseball is hit, run, safe! Stand sideways like a surfer, bat back over your shoulder — then swing the door LEVEL, crack! Drop the bat and run the bases, touch each one, all the way home. And when you play catch after — big glove, fingers up, pull the ball into the pocket."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is baseball — the crack-and-run game."
  2. Build the stance: side-on, feet apart, bat held back over the shoulder like a door waiting to open.
  3. Swing the door: level through the ball on the tee — not down, not up, flat and whooshy. Whoosh three times with no ball.
  4. Then the tee: soft ball, real contact, CRACK — and the bat DROPS, legs go, run!
  5. Play the cushion diamond below and close: "side-on, swing level, run like wind."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "baseball" stands at the top in big letters, the game’s scene below — bat, glove and the flying ball exactly as the sport looks on the diamond.

Ask your child

"Which way does the swing go — down like an axe or around like a door?" "What do we do after the crack?" "What are the four white squares called?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Crack! I hit it!" "I ran all the bases!" or the batter’s secret: "I stand like a surfer!"

Out in the real world

Baseball lives in parks and backyards everywhere — and its little cousin lives on every picnic blanket. Watch a few pitches together and hunt for the level swing: doors, not axes.

Try it together

Cushion Diamond: four cushions as bases around the room, a stool-tee at "home." Hit off the tee (or a gentle grown-up pitch), run touch-touch-touch, home shouts SAFE with both arms out — the fielder’s favourite word. Then swap: fielder catches the next hit. Every child plays both sides, which is the whole sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "Level swing or chopping swing? What do we drop before we run? What do we shout when we reach home?" Level, the bat, SAFE — three answers and the diamond is open.

Parent tips

Rolling a sock around the bat tip slows the swing naturally — heavy-end training, pro-style. And let the tee shrink in height over the weeks: waist, then knee — the level swing learns to find both.

This lesson pairs with the Baseball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cricket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches cricket around one shape: the bat swings straight through the line like a door with a hinge — and the bowling arrives slow enough to love.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Cricket is a bat-and-ball game between two teams: the bowler bowls at three stumps, the batter defends them and hits away, then the pair run. The fielders fetch — a lot.

What does it mean?

Cricket is the patient sport: turn after turn, over after over, the game breathes slowly. For a four-year-old it teaches the longest duel in sport — one bowler, one batter, and the three little sticks that matter to both.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cricket ideas: the bat hangs flat like a door waiting to swing; the straight drive goes through the line of the ball; and bowling is an underarm ROLL first — big, slow and friendly.

Why this matters

Cricket owns half this wall’s map: India, Australia, England, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Caribbean. A four-year-old who can swing straight has joined the biggest after-school club on Earth.

What it teaches

Straight-line striking, the side-on stance with hands together, underarm rolling (the gentler sibling of throwing), and fetching — the fielding half of every bat game.

Words to learn

cricketbatstumpswicketsbowlstraightrun

Say this to your child

“"Cricket is the three-sticks game! The stumps stand behind you like a little castle. Hold the bat flat with both hands, stand side-on, and swing STRAIGHT through the ball — whack! Then you run, and the other team fetches. And when it is your turn to bowl: big gentle underarm, right at the castle."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is cricket — the game with the three little sticks."
  2. Meet the stumps: three tubes standing in a row — the batter’s castle. The bowler’s job is to knock it; the batter’s job is the wall.
  3. Grip and stance: both hands together on the flat bat, side-on, bat hanging down like a door on its hinge.
  4. The straight drive: swing the door straight through the ball’s line — through the gate, not across it. Ten slow swings.
  5. Play backyard wickets below and close: "straight bat, big swing, run the runs."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "cricket" is printed large at the top with the game’s scene underneath — the flat bat, the stumps and the red ball exactly as the game looks on the green.

Ask your child

"What stands behind the batter?" "Which way does the bat swing — across or straight through?" "How does a gentle bowler deliver the ball?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I protected the castle!" "Whack — straight through the gate!" or the bowler’s line: "Big slow underarm, watch this!"

Out in the real world

Cricket is everywhere from Auckland to Adelaide to Ahmedabad — the beach, the street, the park at dusk. Watch ten balls of a real match and call the shape together: straight door, straight swing.

Try it together

Backyard Wickets: three tubes as stumps, a bucket six paces away. Underarm bowl at the castle (one point), then batter swings the straight drive and the pair run one lap of the bucket (two points). Bowling earns, batting earns — the two jobs trade every over, which is cricket’s whole rhythm at knee height.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we defend? Straight swing or cross swing? How does a kind bowler bowl?" The stumps, straight, underarm — three answers and the long game has begun.

Parent tips

A big soft ball and a wide bat keep early swings honest. And teach the bowler first: children who can deliver a friendly ball become the batter everyone wants — and the patience of bowling is the patience of the whole game.

This lesson pairs with the Cricket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rugby — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches rugby around its delightful upside-down rule: the ball only travels backwards — so to score, somebody has to RUN.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Rugby is a running game with an oval ball: carry it in both hands, run forward, and pass only backwards to teammates. Score by grounding the ball past the far line — a try!

What does it mean?

Every other ball sport rewards passing forward — rugby forbids it. That one twist makes running the only way the game moves, which is why rugby players are runners first and passers second, and why the rule alone is a lesson worth an afternoon.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rugby ideas: the ball is carried in TWO hands — hugged, not held; the pass goes BACKWARDS over the shoulder; and in the junior game the tackle is a tag — grab the ribbon, never the body.

Why this matters

Rugby owns this wall’s southern hemisphere: New Zealand’s all blacks haka, Australia’s league and union, South Africa’s springboks. It is also the finest excuse to run Flat Out while hugging a cushion.

What it teaches

Two-hand carrying while running (a real coordination split), the around-the-corner backward pass, evasion running — and in tag versions, the honesty of the tug.

Words to learn

rugbytrypassbackwardscarrytagrun

Say this to your child

“"Rugby is the backwards game! Hug the ball in both arms, run as fast as your legs go — and if you pass, it must go BACKWARDS, over your shoulder, to the friend behind you. Forward pass? No no! Run to the far wall and press the ball down — TRY!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is rugby — the hug-the-ball running game."
  2. The carry: ball (or cushion) hugged in both arms at the chest — not under one arm like a baguette. Jog a lap, hug intact.
  3. The backwards rule: demonstrate forward pass — shake the head! Then the legal one: stop, swing the ball back over the shoulder, partner walking behind catches.
  4. Join them: run forward three steps, pass back, runner receives on the move. The rhythm IS the sport.
  5. Play try-line tag below and close: "hug, run, pass it back."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "rugby" leads at the top in big letters with the game’s scene below — the oval ball carried in both hands exactly as the run looks on the field.

Ask your child

"Can we pass the ball forward?" "How many hands carry the ball?" "What do we shout when we press it down past the line?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Backwards only — that’s the rule!" "I hugged it all the way!" or the try call: "TRY! I pressed it down!"

Out in the real world

Rugby lives in every park in Auckland, Sydney and Cardiff — and on the screen every spring. Watch one try together and count the passes: they all travel backwards. The whole game in one rule.

Try it together

Try-Line Tag: two players with tag-ribbons tucked in the waistband, ball hugged, running the length of the room. The chaser tugs a ribbon — stop, pass BACK over the shoulder to a fresh runner, ribbons reset, go again. Cross the far line, press the ball down, TRY — and the haka dance of your family’s own invention.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which way does a rugby pass go? How many hands on the ball? What is scoring called?" Backwards, two, a try — three answers and the running game is on.

Parent tips

The backward pass feels wrong for about ten minutes, then it feels like the best secret in sport — let the wrongness be funny. And if a real tag belt is missing, a scarf tucked in the waistband works exactly as well.

This lesson pairs with the Rugby flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

American Football — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches American football through its strangest, best toy: the pointed ball that flies funny, wobbles wonderful and demands the best over-arm throw in sport.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

American football is a running-and-throwing game on a long field: one team throws and runs the oval ball downfield, the other chases and tackles (or tags), and crossing the far line scores a touchdown.

What does it mean?

The oval ball is the point of the lesson: it will not bounce straight, it will not fly straight — it demands the fingers lace the points, the arm comes over the top, and the body steps into the throw. The funniest ball teaches the finest throw.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three football ideas: fingers find the LACES for the grip; the throw comes over the top like a rainbow with a spin; and the end zone is the promised land — cross the line, hold the ball tight, TOUCHDOWN.

Why this matters

From Super Bowl Sunday to the schoolyard at recess, this is the sport American children meet first — and its over-arm throw is the single most transferable skill on the wall: baseball throws it, tennis serves it, every dodgeball throws it.

What it teaches

Over-arm throwing at full extension, the lace grip (fine motor), running with purpose to a line, and the caught-in-the-crowd celebration — sport needs its parties.

Words to learn

footballlacesthrowcatchend zonetouchdownrun

Say this to your child

“"American football’s ball is a funny egg! Put your fingers on the laces, bring it back by your ear, step and throw OVER the top — see it spin? Wobble is fine. And when you HUG it and run all the way past the far line and hold it down — that is a TOUCHDOWN, the biggest word in the whole sport!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is American football — the wobbly egg-ball game."
  2. Meet the ball: roll it — it curves! Bounce it — it goes sideways! The oval ball is deliciously disobedient, and that is why it needs special hands.
  3. The lace grip: fingers over the laces, point of the ball peeking past the hand. Hug-carry for runners, laces for throwers.
  4. The throw: ball to the ear, step forward, arm over the TOP — let it spin. Ten throws at a cushion target, wobbles welcome.
  5. Play the end-zone dash below and close: "hug to run, laces to throw, cross the line."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "american football" stand large at the top with the game’s scene below — the brown oval ball exactly as the sport looks on the gridiron.

Ask your child

"Why does this ball fly funny?" "Where do the fingers go?" "What do we shout when we cross the line?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "It wobbles when it flies!" "My fingers found the laces!" or the big one: "TOUCHDOWN!" with both arms up.

Out in the real world

Football lives on every American screen from September to February — watch ONE kickoff return together and spot the three things from today: the hug-carry, the lace-throw, the line-crossing party.

Try it together

End-Zone Dash: two cushions one room apart. Quarterback throws (or hands off) to the runner, who hugs and dodges past a tagger to the far cushion — touchdown, spike the (soft) ball, dance. Swap jobs every play. The thrower throws, the runner runs, the tagger tags — three jobs, one game, everyone loud.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do the fingers go for a throw? Over the top or sidearm? What is the far line called?" Laces, over the top, the end zone — three answers and the wobbly ball flies.

Parent tips

A foam football or even a sock-stuffed sock flies soft and spins true enough for the lesson. And teach the touchdown dance early — in this family, style points count.

This lesson pairs with the American Football flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Hockey — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hockey on the floor first, where nobody slips: the stick becomes a long arm, the ball becomes a pet to herd, and the goal is always two chair-legs away.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Hockey is a team game played with curved sticks: dribble the puck or ball side to side, pass with a push, and shoot for the goal. On ice it is the fastest team sport there is; on a living-room floor it is the same game at four-year-old speed.

What does it mean?

Hockey moves the ball sideways — no other sport on this wall steers with lateral taps. That side-to-side dribble builds wrist control and the quiet discovery that a stick is a lever: push far end, ball goes near end.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three hockey ideas: hands split the stick — one on top, one halfway down; the dribble is little pushes SIDEWAYS, never a big whack; and the shot is one strong push through the ball toward the middle of the goal.

Why this matters

Floor hockey asks for no ice, no rink and no skates — a broom and a sponge ball do it. And the dribble it teaches is the same one field hockey, ice hockey and the golf swing all borrow later.

What it teaches

Lever control (two-handed implement at split grip), lateral tapping accuracy, quick direction changes while herding, and turn-taking in goal.

Words to learn

hockeystickpuckdribblepushshootgoal

Say this to your child

“"Hockey is the stick game! One hand on top, one hand down low — the stick is your extra arm. Push the ball side to side, little pushes, keep it close like a pet on a leash. Then pass it with a push, and when the goal is open — one big push, SHOOT!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is hockey — the stick-and-slide game."
  2. Split the hands: one at the top of the stick, one partway down — the long arm and the steering arm.
  3. The dribble: little sideways pushes, ball stays close — a dog on a short leash. Weave between two chair-cones.
  4. The pass: a firm push with the stick’s flat face to a partner’s stick — hockey passes are pushes, not swings.
  5. Play chair-goal hockey below and close: "low stick, little pushes, big shot."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "hockey" stands big at the top with the game’s scene beneath — the curved sticks and the puck exactly as the game looks on the ice or the floor.

Ask your child

"Where do our two hands go on the stick?" "Big whacks or little pushes?" "What do we call the black disk the stick pushes?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The stick is my extra arm!" "I herded the ball through the cones!" or the shot call: "Push… SHOOT!"

Out in the real world

Hockey lives on ice rinks and in driveways — street hockey, knee hockey on carpets, field hockey on grass. Watch thirty seconds of a real game and count the sideways pushes: the dribble is the whole sport’s heartbeat.

Try it together

Chair-Goal Hockey: two chair-legs as the goal, a broom or pool noodle as the stick, a sponge ball as the puck. Dribble a cone-slalom, then shoot for the chair-mouth. Swap: one shoots, one is the goalkeeper — stick flat, guard the mouth. Goals and saves both get the full roar.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do the hands go? Push or whack? What guards the goal?" Split grip, little pushes, the goalkeeper — three answers and the floor game is on.

Parent tips

Keep every swing below the knee — floor hockey’s one rule, and it protects shins and lamps alike. A rolled-up pair of socks is the perfect first puck: it cannot roll away and cannot hurt anything.

This lesson pairs with the Hockey flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Lacrosse — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches lacrosse from the ground up — literally: the first skill is scooping the ball off the floor into a net, and for many children it is the first catch they ever make easily.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Lacrosse is a team game with a netted pocket on the end of a stick: scoop the ball up, cradle it while you run, pass or shoot with a flick of the stick. It is the oldest sport on this wall — played first by the Haudenosaunee.

What does it mean?

Every catching skill on this wall catches from the front or above. Lacrosse catches from BELOW — the ball drops into the nest. Children whose hands struggle with mid-air catches often shine the moment the stick does the catching.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three lacrosse ideas: the scoop is a shovel motion — stick low, through the ball, up; the cradle is a gentle rocking that keeps the ball nestling while running; and the pass is a flick, like tossing from a salad bowl.

Why this matters

Lacrosse carries two gifts: a catching skill for children who need the ball to slow down, and a story worth telling — the game grew up on this continent long before any of the others arrived.

What it teaches

Scooping from the floor (ground-level tracking), carrying while moving (the cradle is balance plus focus), under-flick accuracy, and the respect-first history of the Creator’s game.

Words to learn

lacrossesticknetscoopcradleflickcarry

Say this to your child

“"Lacrosse sticks have a little net basket! Scoop the ball up off the floor — shloop! — nestle it in the net, and rock it gently while you walk. Cradle, cradle. Then flick it soft as tossing salad to a friend. The stick catches for you — your job is just to keep it rocking."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is lacrosse — the game with the net basket on a stick."
  2. The scoop: stick low like a shovel, push it through the ball along the floor, lift — the ball nests. Five scoops, celebrate each.
  3. The cradle: ball in the pocket, rock the stick gently in and out as you walk — in-out, in-out. It is a lullaby for a ball.
  4. The flick: tip the stick forward softly and toss the ball to a partner’s pocket or a bucket.
  5. Play the scoop relay below and close: "scoop, cradle, flick."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "lacrosse" is printed large at the top with the game’s scene below — the netted stick and the small ball exactly as the game looks on the field.

Ask your child

"What is in the net at the end of the stick?" "How do we pick the ball up?" "What do our arms do while we run with the ball?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The net caught it!" "I cradled it all the way across!" or the scoop cheer: "Shloop — got it!"

Out in the real world

Lacrosse lives in schools and clubs across Canada and the US — and its scoop lives in every kitchen: a spoon lifting cereal is a scoop, a net bag gathering toys is a cradle. The oldest sport is hiding in the chores.

Try it together

Scoop Relay: bucket at one end of the room, five scattered soft balls, stick (or large spoon) in hand. Scoop each ball, cradle it to the bucket, flick it in — five trips, timed by cheering not by clock. Then swap and race a partner gently. The floor is emptied by the nest, and every scoop is a catch.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we lift the ball from the floor? What keeps it in the pocket while we run? What does the pass look like?" Scoop, the cradle, a flick — three answers and the nest is open.

Parent tips

If no stick exists, a milk jug cut into a scoop or a large serving spoon carries the whole lesson. And teach the cradle BEFORE the running — rocking still, then walking, then jogging: the lullaby has three speeds.

This lesson pairs with the Lacrosse flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Handball — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches handball in its three-beat rhythm — run, throw, save — and turns a doorway into the most shot-at goal in the house.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Handball is a team game where hands do everything: run with the ball (three steps at our size), bounce it if you like, then throw it into the goal. The goalkeeper stands tall with arms wide to stop it.

What does it mean?

Handball’s throw is the strongest one-arm throw in sport — a leap, a whip, a finish. At four-year-old scale it becomes the best throwing practice on this wall: a real target, a real keeper, and permission to throw AT something at last.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three handball ideas: three steps is the rule of the game — run three, throw or bounce; the goal shot is one arm, big and high, aimed at the corners; and the keeper is a starfish — feet spread, arms wide, wobble allowed.

Why this matters

Every child wants to throw at a target; every parent wants the target to be soft and the rules short. Handball is that wish granted: three steps, one throw, and the world’s most dramatic save pose.

What it teaches

One-arm throwing with trunk rotation (the power pattern all throws grow from), stepping to a line under excitement, and the keeper’s read — watching a ball, then meeting it.

Words to learn

handballthrowgoalthree stepskeepersavecorner

Say this to your child

“"Handball is the three-step game! Run step-step-step — no more! — then one BIG throw with one arm at the goal. Pick your corner, not the middle. And when you are the keeper: feet wide, arms up, be a starfish! Every save is worth a goal, and every goal is worth a starfish."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is handball — the run-three-steps-and-throw game."
  2. The three-step rule: walk it out loud — step, step, step… THROW or BOUNCE. The rule is the game’s heartbeat; practise it dry first.
  3. The goal shot: one arm, big circle back, step into it, finish pointing at the corner you chose. Corners beat middles — that is the aiming lesson.
  4. The starfish save: feet wide, arms up like a big X, body behind the ball. Practise three saves from gentle throws.
  5. Play doorway handball below and close: "three steps, one throw, starfish saves."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "handball" leads at the top in big letters with the game’s scene underneath — the flying throw at the goal exactly as the sport looks on the court.

Ask your child

"How many steps can we run?" "One arm or two for the goal shot?" "What shape is the goalkeeper?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Three steps, then I throw!" "I hit the top corner!" or the keeper’s cry: "STARFISH — saved it!"

Out in the real world

Handball owns playgrounds across Europe — and its three-step spirit lives in every hallway game of throw-the-sock-into-the-hamper. Watch one fast-break goal together and count the steps: step, step, step, throw.

Try it together

Doorway Handball: the doorway (or two cushion towers) is the goal, a soft ball, keeper in starfish. Attacker runs three steps from the corridor and throws for a corner; keeper saves or concedes with full drama. Trade places every throw. Three rules total: three steps, pads-soft ball, and the keeper may wobble.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many steps before we throw? Which arm throws at goal? What is the keeper’s shape?" Three, one arm, a starfish — three answers and the doorway is a stadium.

Parent tips

Corners are hard to hit and easy to love — praise the AIMED miss more than the lucky middle. And let the keeper lie down dramatically after each goal; goalkeeping is theatre, and four-year-olds know it.

This lesson pairs with the Handball flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Golf — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches golf as the wall’s whisper: where hockey pushes and baseball whips, golf swings SLOW — and counts every tap on the way to the hole.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Golf is a target game on a very big course: swing the club, send the small ball toward the hole, and count how many strokes it takes. Fewest taps wins — and slow swings beat strong ones every time.

What does it mean?

Golf is the control sport. Every other card rewards force; golf rewards restraint — the smoother the swing, the straighter the ball. For a four-year-old that is a brand-new idea: sometimes the body wins by slowing down.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three golf ideas: hands hold the club like two friends sharing one handle; the swing is a pendulum — back slow, through slower; and every tap is a COUNT — the counting is not extra, it is the game.

Why this matters

Aiming small and swinging slow grows the precision end of fundamental movement skills — the twin of the big-power skills every other ball game drills. Golf is where the body learns whisper control.

What it teaches

Pendulum swinging (pendulum rhythm is a timing skill all its own), small-target aiming, stroke counting — early maths on the fairway — and the patience of trying again calmly.

Words to learn

golfclubswingputtholestrokecount

Say this to your child

“"Golf is the whisper game! Hold the club like two friends sharing one umbrella. Swing slow — back like a clock, through like a clock, whoooosh. The tiny ball rolls and rolls… and we count every tap: one, two, THREE — in the hole! Fewest taps wins, and slow is the secret."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is golf — the slow-swing counting game."
  2. The grip: both hands together on the handle, thumbs down the middle — two friends sharing an umbrella.
  3. The pendulum: swing back like a clock hand… and through like a clock hand — smooth, no chopping. Whoooosh, not WHACK.
  4. Putt first: the tiny swing on the carpet, ball rolling to a cup. Count every tap out loud: one… two… three — in the cup!
  5. Play carpet golf below and close: "slow swing, small ball, keep counting."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "golf" stands at the top in big letters with the game’s scene below — the club, the small white ball and the green exactly as the game looks on the course.

Ask your child

"Fast swing or slow swing?" "What do we count?" "How do our hands hold the club?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Whoosh — slow like a clock!" "Three taps and I sank it!" or the golfer’s whisper: "Gentle… gentle… in!"

Out in the real world

Golf lives at courses, driving ranges and mini-golf parks — the mini-putt course is a child’s paradise built exactly on today’s skill. Walk one together and count strokes per hole like the pros.

Try it together

Carpet Golf: a bucket or cup at one end of the carpet, a spoon-club, a pom-pom ball. Stroke one: tap. Stroke two: tap. Sink it in three — par for the living room! Lay a "course" of three cups with sofa-cushion hazards between. The scorecard can be drawn; the counting must be loud.

Understanding check

Ask: "Whack or whoosh? What do we count after every tap? What wins the game?" Whoosh, the strokes, fewest taps — three answers and the whisper game is on.

Parent tips

Make the child the scoreboard — counting strokes is maths practice smuggled into sport. And if the swing keeps chopping, hold a balloon above the clubhead: a swing that pops it is chopping; a swing that never touches is a true pendulum.

This lesson pairs with the Golf flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Athletics — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches athletics in its three honest words — run, jump, throw — the exact three New Zealand and Australian schools call the heart of movement, and the three every four-year-old is already in love with.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Athletics is track and field: sprints and distance running on the track, long jumps and high jumps in the field, throws of every weight — all of it measured, all of it cheered, all of it built from skills children meet in the backyard first.

What does it mean?

Athletics is the mother of sports: nearly every ball game on this wall borrows its run, its jump or its throw. Done on its own, it needs no team, no ball and no rules longer than a breath — the purest gross motor sport there is.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three athletics ideas: the sprint begins with a crouch and a WAIT for the word go; the long jump is knees bent, arms swing, TWO feet off together; and the throw turns the whole body side-on and lets the arm arrive last.

Why this matters

Run, jump, throw is the exact phrase NZ’s and Australia’s school curriculums use for fundamental movement skills — teaching the three words explicitly gives a child the keys to every sport that follows.

What it teaches

Sprint acceleration, two-foot take-off with arm swing, side-on throwing with trunk rotation — the three pillars — plus measuring: how far is a really good day?

Words to learn

athleticssprintjumpthrowtrackfieldmeasure

Say this to your child

“"Athletics is three games in one! Crouch down for the sprint — wait for GO, then fly. Bend your knees for the long jump — swing the arms, two feet, FROG! Then turn sideways for the throw — big circle, let it fly, how many footsteps did it go? Run, jump, throw: that is the Olympics of the backyard."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is athletics — running, jumping and throwing, the Olympic games."
  2. The sprint: crouch low, fingers on the line, freeze… then GO on the word. Practise the waiting — the crouch is half the race.
  3. The long jump: bend the knees, swing the arms BACK then UP, two feet leave together, land like a frog. Measure each jump with a shoe.
  4. The throw: stand side-on, weight back, big arm circle, release pointing at the sky’s window — measure with footsteps.
  5. Run the three-station mini-meet below and close: "crouch, bend, turn — go!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "athletics" is printed big at the top with the game’s scene beneath — the track, the lane lines and the runner exactly as a race day looks.

Ask your child

"What do we do while we wait at the sprint line?" "Do we jump off one foot or two?" "Which way does our body face for a big throw?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I waited… then ZOOM!" "My frog jump went two shoes!" or the thrower’s report: "It flew six footsteps!"

Out in the real world

Athletics owns every school sports day in the US, Canada, Australia and NZ — and the Olympics bring the whole wall to life every four years. Watch one long jump together and find the three beats: bend, swing, frog.

Try it together

Three-Station Meet: chalk a sprint lane, a jump line and a throw zone. One minute at each — sprint out and back, three frog jumps measured in shoes, one mighty bean-bag throw measured in footsteps. Write the "records" on paper, cheer absurdly, and hand out a drawn medal. That is a real athletics meet, scaled for four legs.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three athletics words? What waits at the sprint line? How do we land the long jump?" Run-jump-throw, a crouch, like a frog — three answers and the meet is open.

Parent tips

Measure everything — shoes, footsteps, books. The measuring is what turns running around into ATHLETICS, and comparing your own record to yesterday’s is the healthiest competition there is.

This lesson pairs with the Athletics flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Gymnastics — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches gymnastics as the wall’s quiet king: no ball, no net, no goal — just a body learning to make shapes and hold them still.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Gymnastics is the sport of body control: balances on feet and hands, shapes made with straight arms and pointed toes, rolls across the mats, and swings on bars — every move practised slowly until it looks easy.

What does it mean?

Balance is the skill every other sport silently borrows — the skater, the batter, the karate kid all stand on one leg in the end. Gymnastics trains it on purpose, slowly, which is why gymnasts pick up every other game faster.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three gymnastics ideas: the star shape is arms AND legs wide, held like a superhero landing; the log roll keeps the body STRAIGHT while it turns; and the balance asks for stillness — wobble is part of the work, not the failure.

Why this matters

Of everything on this wall, gymnastics is the most transferable hour a four-year-old can spend: grip, balance, falling safely and the bravery of trying a new shape all live here before anywhere else.

What it teaches

Static balance, body-shape awareness (straight, tucked, wide), rolling — the first safe-fall skill — and the focus of holding still while everything wants to wiggle.

Words to learn

gymnasticsbalanceshaperollstillholdmat

Say this to your child

“"Gymnastics is making your body into shapes! Star shape — arms wide, legs wide, hold it like a superhero. Pencil shape — body straight, arms squeezed past your ears, tippy-toes. And the log roll — straight as a pencil, roll across the mat like a falling tree. Wobbles are allowed; stillness is the treasure."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is gymnastics — the game of making shapes with your body."
  2. The star: arms up wide, legs apart, hold for three slow counts — superhero landing, eyes forward. Wobbling counts as trying.
  3. The pencil: body STRAIGHT, arms squeezed to the ears, stand on tiptoe — the tallest shape there is.
  4. The log roll: lie straight as a pencil on the bed or mat, arms up, and roll across — the body never bends. Three rolls, giggles mandatory.
  5. Play shape-freeze below and close: "make the shape, hold it still, ta-da."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "gymnastics" leads at the top in big letters with the game’s scene underneath — the balancing child with arms out exactly as a class on the mats looks.

Ask your child

"What shapes can your body make?" "What does the log roll keep straight?" "Is wobbling okay?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I held the star for five!" "I rolled like a pencil!" or the gymnast’s bow: "Ta-da!"

Out in the real world

Gymnastics lives in every soft-play centre and school hall — and its shapes live in every living room: the superhero landing, the tip-toe reach for the biscuit tin, the log roll across the big bed. Shapes everywhere.

Try it together

Shape-Freeze: call a shape — STAR! PENCIL! TUCK (knees hugged)! — and freeze in it. Three counts of stillness earns a point; a giggle-collapse earns a retry. Then the balance beam: a line of tape on the floor, heel-to-toe, arms out, and a proper gymnast finish — arms up, one knee, ta-da. The living room becomes the podium.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name a gymnastics shape. What stays straight in a log roll? Is it better to hold still or wiggle?" Star (or pencil), the body, hold still — three answers and the mats are open.

Parent tips

Practise on something soft and celebrate the wobble — stillness grows out of wobbles, never out of scolding. And teach the safety roll (chin tucked, roll on shoulders) as THE way to fall; it is judo’s gift hiding inside gymnastics.

This lesson pairs with the Gymnastics flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Marathon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the marathon’s one big secret: the race is not won by the fastest legs but by the legs that never stop — pacing is a skill, and four is a fine age to start it.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

A marathon is a running race of 42.195 kilometres — a whole day on your feet. Nobody sprints it: marathoners jog at one steady speed for hours, drinking water at little tables, cheered by whole cities, and finishing is the victory.

What does it mean?

Four-year-olds are sprinters by nature: all burst, no battery. The marathon card teaches the opposite muscle — the keep-going muscle — and it does it in the friendliest unit there is: one lap, then one more.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three marathon ideas: marathoners go SLOW on purpose — steady beats speedy when the road is long; water breaks are part of the race, not a timeout from it; and the finish line is for EVERYONE who keeps stepping.

Why this matters

Stamina is the quietest fundamental movement skill — hidden inside every long playground morning. Naming it, counting laps and celebrating the finish turns I’m tired into one more step, which is a life skill wearing a race bib.

What it teaches

Aerobic stamina in tiny doses, pace self-regulation (the hardest skill in the lesson), lap counting, and the finish-line feeling — effort followed by enormous pride.

Words to learn

marathonracepacesteadylapfinish linemedal

Say this to your child

“"The marathon is the longest race there is — 42 kilometres, a whole day of running! Nobody rushes it. Steady steps, one foot, other foot, sip of water, keep going. And when you finally cross the finish line — even in last place — the whole city cheers, because you KEPT GOING. That is the marathon’s secret: finishing is winning."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the marathon — the longest race in the world."
  2. The distance: 42 kilometres — walk it out: "that is walking ALL DAY." Ask what you would need to bring. (Water! Shoes! Patience!)
  3. The pace secret: sprint across the room — done in five seconds, breath gone. Then jog-slow the same room — still going. THAT is marathon running: slow enough to keep going.
  4. The water table: marathoners drink WHILE racing — practise the funny walk-and-sip.
  5. Play the living-room marathon below and close: "steady steps, one more, finish line."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "marathon" stands big at the top with the race’s scene below — the runner, the road and the finish exactly as the long race looks on the day.

Ask your child

"Is a marathon short or long?" "Do marathoners run fast the whole way?" "What do they drink on the way?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Slow and steady keeps going!" "I did twelve laps!" or the finish call: "I made it — where is my medal?"

Out in the real world

Marathons close real streets in real cities — New York, Boston, Auckland, Sydney — and the crowds cheer every single finisher. Watch the last runner cross a real finish line together: the loudest cheer of the day belongs to the last pair of legs.

Try it together

Living-Room Marathon: pick a lap (hallway loop or garden circuit), agree a steady pace — no sprinting, that is the one rule — and count laps out loud. Five laps: water break at the "table." Ten laps: finish line of two chairs, tape across, break through it, medal drawn on the spot. The stamina is small, the ceremony is huge.

Understanding check

Ask: "How long is a marathon? What is the secret speed? What happens when you finish the race?" Very long, slow and steady, a big cheer and a medal — three answers and the keep-going muscle grows.

Parent tips

Keep laps tiny and ceremony enormous — stamina grows on reps of pride, not distance. And if the child suddenly sprints and bonks, that IS the lesson: ask how their legs feel now versus the steady laps. The body explains pacing better than any lecture.

This lesson pairs with the Marathon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Triathlon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the triathlon’s wonderful idea — three sports stacked into one race — and practises the strangest skill in it: changing from one kind of moving to another without stopping.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

A triathlon is one race with three legs: swim first, then cycle, then run to the finish. In between are the transitions — where athletes swap goggles for helmets for shoes as fast as they can.

What does it mean?

The triathlon’s hidden skill is the switch: arms doing crawl one minute, then steering handlebars, then pumping as legs. Switching movement styles mid-game is real coordination training — the brain rebuilds its plan at speed.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three triathlon ideas: the order never changes — swim, bike, run; the transition is part of the race (no sitting around in the middle!); and tri means three — the word itself is a lesson.

Why this matters

Of all the cards on the wall, this one mixes the most skills into one game — crawl arms, pedalling legs, sprinting feet — which makes it the perfect grand finale for a morning of movement play.

What it teaches

Skill-switching (the real star), sequencing a multi-part plan, transition speed, and the endurance of doing three things before asking for a snack.

Words to learn

triathlonthreeswimbikeruntransitionfinish

Say this to your child

“"The triathlon is three races glued together! First SWIM — windmill arms through the sofa-sea. Then BIKE — pedalling legs round and round. Then RUN — light feet to the finish! And the funniest part is the swap in the middle, the transition: goggles off, helmet on, GO GO GO!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is the triathlon — three races in one."
  2. Decode the word: TRI means three — triangle, tricycle, triathlon. What comes in threes?
  3. The three legs: swim arms (big windmills), bike legs (round and round), run feet (fast and light). Practise each for ten seconds.
  4. The transition: the magic moment — arms stop swimming, hands grab handlebars. Announce it like a race commentator: "AND SHE’S ON THE BIKE!"
  5. Play the living-room triathlon below and close: "swim, bike, run — nothing stops in between."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "triathlon" is printed large at the top with the race’s scene below — the swim, the bike and the run exactly as the three-leg race looks.

Ask your child

"What does TRI mean?" "What are the three legs, in order?" "What is the swap in the middle called?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Swim, then bike, then run!" "I did all three!" or the commentator’s cry: "AND SHE’S ON THE BIKE!"

Out in the real world

Triathlons happen in every city with a lake and a road — and kids’ versions (splash, pedal, dash) exist in most towns each summer. Watch one transition zone together: shoes, helmets, chaos — the funniest minute in sport.

Try it together

Living-Room Triathlon: sofa cushions are the sea (crawl on tummies), a hobby-horse or trike loop is the bike leg, and the corridor is the run to the finish tape. Commentate every leg, time the transitions, medal the finisher. Add a second competitor for a real race — the toys may enter.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three legs in order. What do we call the swap? What does tri mean?" Swim-bike-run, the transition, three — three answers and the race is on.

Parent tips

Keep each leg SHORT — the joy is in the switching, not the distance. And let the child be the commentator once: shouting "AND SHE’S ON THE BIKE" teaches the sequence better than any diagram.

This lesson pairs with the Triathlon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Cycling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches cycling from the pedal up: the round-and-round motion the legs must learn, the glide the balance bike gives for free, and the helmet rule that starts with the very first ride.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Cycling is riding a two-wheeled machine: push the pedals round, steer with the handlebars, and balance on two wheels while the world rolls past. It is also every child’s first taste of real speed under their own power.

What does it mean?

The pedal stroke is a genuine coordination puzzle: one leg pushes down while the other lifts up, both going in CIRCLES — not the up-down stomping legs want to do. Training the circle first is the whole trick.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three cycling ideas: pedals go in CIRCLES — round and round, never stampy-stampy; the glide is the secret inside every bike — scoot, lift the feet, WHOOSH; and the helmet goes on before the wheels do, every single time.

Why this matters

Cycling is the first freedom machine: the day the child outruns the grown-up is a family memory. And the safety habit worn at four — helmet, every ride — is the same habit that keeps riders safe at fourteen.

What it teaches

Circular leg coordination (a distinct skill from walking), dynamic balance via gliding, steering-hands and looking-eyes working together, and the non-negotiable safety routine.

Words to learn

cyclingbikepedalhelmetbalanceglidesteer

Say this to your child

“"Cycling is driving your very own machine! First the helmet — click, that is the rule, every ride. Then the pedals: round and ROUND in circles, like stirring a giant pot with your feet. And when the bike starts to glide — scoot, feet up, WHOOSH — that is you, balancing all by yourself, going faster than your grown-up!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is cycling — the machine YOU drive."
  2. Air-cycling: lie on the back, legs in the air, pedal round and round like riding an invisible bike — circles, not stamps. Sing a pedalling song if one appears.
  3. The glide: on a balance bike (or any scoot), push with the feet, then LIFT them — the bike glides on its own. Glide is balance’s teacher.
  4. The helmet ritual: helmet ON before wheels touch ground, buckle clicked, two-finger check under the chin. Make it the same ritual every time — a ceremony, not a nag.
  5. Play the pedal-circle game below and close: "circles, glide, helmet on."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "cycling" leads at the top in big letters with the ride’s scene below — the child, the bike and the helmet exactly as the first ride looks.

Ask your child

"Which way do pedals go — circles or stamps?" "What goes on your head before every ride?" "What happens when you lift your feet and let the bike roll?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Round and round, not stampy!" "Helmet clicked!" or the glide report: "I glided ALL the way to the gate!"

Out in the real world

Bikes live in every garage, driveway and park path in the four countries this class calls home — and the Tour de France brings the big version to the screen each July. Watch thirty seconds together and find the circles: round and round, even uphill.

Try it together

Pedal-Circle Race: two racers lie back-to-back, legs in the air, and air-cycle while a song plays — the pedal that keeps CIRCLES the longest wins (stamping is out!). Then outside or down the hall: balance-bike glide course — scoot, lift, glide between two cones, longest glide is champion. Ceremony for the champion: helmet worn, arms raised, bell rung.

Understanding check

Ask: "What shape do our legs make on the pedals? What do we wear every ride? What is the magic move on a balance bike?" Circles, a helmet, the glide — three answers and the wheels are ready.

Parent tips

If pedals frustrate, park them: balance-bike gliding teaches ALL the balance and none of the stress — many children pedal within a week of mastering the glide. And the helmet ritual works best when the grown-up’s helmet clicks too, every time.

This lesson pairs with the Cycling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Swimming — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches swimming in three dry-land pieces — kick, reach, bubble — so that the pool, when it comes, is a reunion instead of a surprise.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Swimming is moving through water: legs flutter-kick, arms windmill-reach, and the face learns to blow bubbles instead of breathing in. It is a sport, a life skill, and the number one safety skill a small person can own.

What does it mean?

Water is a whole new world for a body: it holds you up, slows you down and gets up your nose. Breaking swimming into three dry-land pieces lets the body learn each one where it is calm — the water then just joins the pieces together.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three swimming ideas: the kick comes from the HIP, small and fast — splashy little flutters, not big slow stomps; the arms are windmills — big slow circles that reach far; and the mouth blows bubbles — out into the water, never in.

Why this matters

Swim schools across the US, Canada, Australia and NZ all start the same way — kick, reach, bubble — because those three pieces ARE swimming. And the safety rule sits underneath every lesson: water is fun WITH a grown-up, never alone.

What it teaches

Hip-driven kicking, cross-pattern arm circles (the crawl pattern), breath control (blowing out is a real self-regulation skill), and the safety habit of checking for the grown-up before every splash.

Words to learn

swimmingkickreachbubblegogglesfloatwater safety

Say this to your child

“"Swimming is how we move through water! Little fast kicks from your hips — splish splash splish. Big windmill arms that reach far far forward. And when your face goes in — blow bubbles OUT, big breath first. And the most important rule in the whole world of water: we NEVER swim without a grown-up. Never never. Say it with me."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is swimming — moving through the water."
  2. The flutter kick: lie on the tummy on a bed or mat, legs out — little fast kicks from the HIP, splashy as a dolphin tail. Ten seconds of kicking to a song.
  3. The windmill arms: standing, big slow arm circles that REACH as far as they can — reach, pull, reach, pull. Then both arms take turns like a wheel.
  4. The bubble: practise on dry land — big breath in, hum and blow OUT slowly. In the bath: chin in, blow bubbles. Mouth out-in, never in-in.
  5. Say the safety rule together, then play the swim-school game below: "never swim without a grown-up."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "swimming" stands at the top in big letters with the water’s scene below — the swimmer, the goggles and the blue exactly as a lesson day at the pool looks.

Ask your child
