"Where does the kick start — knees or hips?" "What shape do the arms make?" "What do we blow in the water?" "And who do we NEVER swim without?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Kick kick kick — splashy!" "I blowed bubbles!" or the safety vow: "Never without a grown-up!"

Out in the real world

Swimming lives at pools, beaches, lakes and the bathtub. Visit the pool and hunt for the three pieces in real swimmers: flutter kicks, windmill arms, bubble streams. The bathtub is the nightly training ground — bubbles on command.

Try it together

Swim School (dry land): towel "towelie" on the head, then the three stations — flutter kick lying down, windmill arms standing, bubble-breath humming. Then the bath or shallow pool: kick the water wild, blow three bubbles, float like a starfish with grown-up hands under the back. Every session ends with the rule, whispered like a spell: never swim without a grown-up.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the flutter kick come from? What do the arms draw? What do we blow? Who do we never swim without?" Hips, windmills, bubbles, a grown-up — four answers and the water is a friend.

Parent tips

Blowing OUT is the skill inside the bubble — children who can hum-and-blow on land transfer it to water within a visit. And let the goggles do their magic: a child who can see underwater stays twice as long, learns twice as fast.

This lesson pairs with the Swimming flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Diving — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches diving where every real diving lesson starts: on dry land, making the shape — arms squeezing ears, body straight as a pencil — long before any water is near.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Diving is entering the water hands first, body straight and tight, so the splash is tiny and the entry is clean. From the poolside hop to the ten-metre tower, every dive is the same beautiful shape in the air.

What does it mean?

The pencil shape is a body-control marvel: straight arms squeezed to ears, tight tummy, pointed toes, held while the whole body moves. It is gymnastics’ shapes with courage added — and it is 100% teachable on the carpet.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three diving ideas: the shape is a pencil — arms locked past the ears, body long, toes pointed; hands enter FIRST and the rest of the body follows through the same hole; and diving only ever happens in DEEP water, where a grown-up says it is allowed.

Why this matters

The pencil shape doubles as the safest fall in sport and the proudest pose on the poolside — and building it on cushions makes the courage grow at home, at four, with zero water risk.

What it teaches

Body alignment under movement (the straightest line the body ever makes), courage sequencing — shape, hold, commit — plus the deep-water-only rule that keeps diving safe.

Words to learn

divingpencilstraightentrysplashdeep waterbrave

Say this to your child

“"Diving is entering the water like a dart! Arms squeeze your ears, body straight as a pencil, tippy-toes — hands go in FIRST and the whole body follows through the same little hole. Splash? What splash! And the diving rule: only in DEEP water, only when a grown-up says — shallow water is where heads bump. Say the rule with me."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is diving — going into the water hands first, straight as a pencil."
  2. Build the pencil: arms up, hands together, squeeze them past the ears, body tall, tummy tight, tippy-toes. Hold three counts. That shape IS the dive.
  3. The entry order: hands first — the pencil goes in the water like a dart, not like a starfish flop.
  4. Dry-land dive: stand on a cushion "platform," make the pencil, lean slowly forward, and fall straight as a dart onto the sofa. Shape held all the way down, every time.
  5. Say the deep-water rule, then play the dive-school game below: "diving is for deep water, with a grown-up."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "diving" stands big at the top with the pool’s scene below — the diver straight as an arrow above the water exactly as the entry looks from the poolside.

Ask your child

"What shape does a diver make?" "What goes into the water first?" "Where is diving allowed — shallow or deep water?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Pencil shape — arms past my ears!" "Hands first, then whoosh!" or the safety vow: "Only deep water, only with a grown-up!"

Out in the real world

Diving lives at every pool with a deep end — and on the Olympics’ most beautiful screens. Watch one slow-motion dive together and find the pencil: arms past ears, toes pointed, one straight line from fingers to splash.

Try it together

Dive School (dry land): cushion platform, sofa "water." Make the pencil, hold it, lean, dive straight — held the whole way. Score the shape, not the landing: straight arms past ears? Toes pointed? Then the pool, someday soon, returns a dart-clean entry the shape already knows.

Understanding check

Ask: "What shape is the dive? What enters first? Where is diving allowed?" The pencil, the hands, deep water with a grown-up — three answers and the shape is ready.

Parent tips

Never rush the water part — the cushion dive holds the whole lesson, and children who own the shape on land find it again in the pool the first time a teacher says pencil. The deep-water rule is non-negotiable and belongs in every repetition, out loud.

This lesson pairs with the Diving flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Water Polo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches water polo’s magic trick: hands busy passing while the LEGS do all the floating — the egg-beater whir that keeps a whole team upright in deep water.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Water polo is a team ball game played floating: tread water, pass with one hand, shoot at the goal, sprint back. The legs whirl like an egg-beater under the surface while the arms do the busy work.

What does it mean?

Water polo splits the body’s jobs in half — legs float, arms play — which is exactly the split swimmers need to grow. Treading water with hands out of the water is one of the deepest water-confidence skills there is.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three water-polo ideas: the egg-beater is legs whirling in little circles under you, like stirring two pots; the scull is hands sweeping out-and-in at the sides, pressing the water down; and the pass is ONE hand — a throw, not a push.

Why this matters

Treading water is the hidden life skill inside the sport — the skill that lets a swimmer stop, look around and rest in deep water. Polo teaches it while playing catch, which is the gentlest way a scary skill was ever learned.

What it teaches

Egg-beater leg coordination (a new pattern distinct from the flutter kick), sculling hand pressure, one-arm throwing from floating, and deep-water confidence in games-sized doses.

Words to learn

water polotreadegg-beaterscullpassgoaldeep end

Say this to your child

“"Water polo is catch-and-throw while you float! Your legs whirl underneath like an egg-beater — stir stir stir — and your hands sweep the water down, down, to hold you up. Then one hand grabs the ball and THROWS it to your teammate. Legs do the floating, hands do the playing — that is the whole secret. And we learn it in shallow water first, always with a grown-up."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is water polo — catch and throw while you FLOAT."
  2. The egg-beater: sitting up in the bath or shallow pool, legs whirl little circles beneath — stir, stir — while the chest stays proud. Practise dry first: sit on the bed edge, legs whirling.
  3. The scull: arms out at the sides, sweep the water out and in, press DOWN to lift the chest. It is how the hands help the legs float.
  4. The one-hand pass: throw (not push) a soft ball to a partner’s chest — one arm, the other one sculling.
  5. Say the deep-water rule, then play the floating pass game below: "legs whirl, hands play."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "water polo" stand large at the top with the pool’s scene below — the floating players and the flying ball exactly as the game looks in the deep end.

Ask your child

"What are the legs doing while the hands play?" "Which hand throws the pass?" "Where does the body stay while all this happens?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "My legs are an egg-beater!" "I threw with ONE hand!" or the proud float: "My hands played while my legs floated!"

Out in the real world

Water polo lives in every city pool with a deep end — and its egg-beater lives at every swim school as the deep-water safety skill. In the bath tonight: legs whirling, chest proud, hands sweeping — the whole sport, knee-deep.

Try it together

Floating Pass: in shallow water (or the bath), sit tall with legs whirling and hands sculling; a partner tosses soft balls one at a time — catch, one-hand pass back. Five catches each, then swap thrower and floater. Dry-land version: bed-edge egg-beater legs, cushion passes. The legs learn to hold, the hands learn to play — the split that makes deep water friendly.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the legs doing under the water? What do the hands do at the sides? How many hands pass the ball? Who do we learn in the deep end with?" Egg-beater, sculling, one, a grown-up — four answers and the deep end gets closer.

Parent tips

Practise the egg-beater dry, again and again — the pattern is odd enough that land reps pay off fast in water. And keep the deep-water rule attached to every mention of the deep end: shallow first, grown-up always, deep someday with the whir already humming.

This lesson pairs with the Water Polo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Surfing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches surfing where every surf school starts: on the floor, doing the pop-up — the one jump that turns a paddler into a rider — long before the ocean gets a vote.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Surfing is riding a board on a moving wave: paddle out past the break, turn, paddle hard as the wave lifts you, then POP UP to standing and ride it to the sand.

What does it mean?

The pop-up is a push-up that ends in a crouch — one explosive move from lying to standing. Practised on the carpet it builds the exact arm push, foot swap and low stance that real waves demand, with zero salt water required.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three surfing ideas: the pop-up is hands-down, feet-in, one hop — like a frog with a plan; the stance is sideways, knees soft, arms out like a tightrope walker; and the leash goes on the ankle first — the board is your buddy, never let it fly free.

Why this matters

Surfing is the balance card with adventure attached: the floor is never still, and the child who can pop up and hold a low stance on land owns the sport’s whole first lesson before the first wave.

What it teaches

Explosive push-to-stand (the pop-up is a genuine power move), low dynamic balance, side-on stance awareness, and the ocean respect that every beach family teaches: waves are strong, grown-ups watch, never turn your back.

Words to learn

surfingwavepaddlepop upstancebalanceleash

Say this to your child

“"Surfing is standing on the water! Paddle out with big arm reaches — paddle, paddle. When the wave lifts the board, POP UP: hands down, feet in, jump low! Knees soft, arms out, ride the wave all the way in. And the beach rules: the leash goes on your ankle so the board never flies away, and we always surf where the grown-ups watch."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is surfing — standing on a board on a moving wave."
  2. Paddle first: lie on the tummy, one arm at a time reaching far forward — paddle, paddle, paddle. This is how surfers travel.
  3. The pop-up: hands flat under the shoulders, push UP, jump the feet in and land LOW — knees bent, sideways stance, arms out. A frog with a plan. Ten pop-ups, slow ones fine.
  4. Hold the ride: once up, FREEZE in the low stance for three counts — that freeze is the ride.
  5. Say the beach rules, then play the wave game below: "pop up, ride low, leash on."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "surfing" is printed large at the top with the wave’s scene underneath — the rider on the board and the blue wave exactly as the ride looks from the sand.

Ask your child

"What do we do before the pop-up?" "Are the knees stiff or soft?" "What goes on the ankle, and why?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Paddle paddle — POP UP!" "I held my ride for three!" or the beach rule: "Leash on — the board is my buddy!"

Out in the real world

Surfing lives at every beach break in Australia, NZ and California — and kids’ board lessons start with exactly this carpet pop-up. Watch one surfer catch a wave together and call the three beats: paddle, pop, ride low.

Try it together

Cushion Waves: a wobbly cushion is the board, the carpet is the sea. Paddle on the tummy three reaches, pop up, hold the low stance three counts — RIDE! Then wobble the cushion gently with a toe while the surfer stays soft-kneed. Every fall is a wipeout, every wipeout is a laugh, every pop-up is the whole sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "What are the three beats — paddle, and then? Are the knees soft or stiff? What stops the board flying away?" Pop up and ride, soft, the leash — three answers and the wave is caught.

Parent tips

Do the pop-ups on carpet in socks — slides are the point, slips are the giggle. And teach the ocean’s golden rule early and forever: waves are stronger than everyone; we swim and surf only where the watching grown-up says.

This lesson pairs with the Surfing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Rowing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches rowing’s three-beat stroke and its deeper lesson: the boat only moves when EVERYBODY moves — in time, all together, one crew.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Rowing is propelling a long thin boat with oars: legs push, body leans back, arms pull the water past — dip, pull, glide — over and over, facing backwards, in perfect time with the crew.

What does it mean?

Rowing is the wall’s one pulling sport: nearly everything else throws and pushes. And its rhythm is its rule — out-of-time strokes chop the boat, in-time strokes make it fly. Togetherness is not a bonus skill here; it is the engine.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three rowing ideas: the stroke has three beats — lean forward, pull back, glide; the legs start the power and the arms finish it; and the whole crew rows IN TIME — that is why rowers count out loud.

Why this matters

Pulling strength is the rarest skill on this wall, and crew rhythm is the purest teamwork game there is — two gifts in one boat, learnable on a carpet with a towel.

What it teaches

Pulling strength (rows are the mirror of every push), sequenced power — legs, body, arms — and synchronised rhythm with a partner, the earliest real crew experience.

Words to learn

rowingoarstrokepullcrewrhythmglide

Say this to your child

“"Rowing is the together game in a long thin boat! Lean forward, pull the oars back, and glide — lean, pull, glide. The legs push first, the arms finish, and everybody does it AT THE SAME TIME — that is why rowers count out loud: one, two, pull! When the crew is in time, the boat flies. When it is not — splashy chaos!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is rowing — one boat, one crew, all together."
  2. The three beats: sit tall, LEAN forward, PULL back, GLIDE. Say it in a whisper-rhythm: lean… pull… glide…
  3. Leg power first: the push starts in the legs, the arms finish — legs, body, arms, in that order. Practise the order slowly.
  4. Backwards view: rowers face where they CAME from — ask why. (Because the pull is easier backwards! And the cox faces forward to steer.)
  5. Play the crew game below and close: "lean, pull, glide — all together."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "rowing" leads at the top in big letters with the water’s scene below — the long boat, the oars and the crew exactly as the race looks from the bank.

Ask your child

"What are the three beats of the stroke?" "Which way does a rower face?" "What happens if the crew rows out of time?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Lean, pull, glide!" "Rowers sit backwards — funny!" or the crew call: "All together — NOW!"

Out in the real world

Rowing lives on rivers in every school town — Oxford and Cambridge race it, Boston and Melbourne row it. Watch one eight glide past together and listen for the count: the boat has a heartbeat and it is the crew’s count.

Try it together

Crew Towel Row: sit on the floor facing a partner, both holding one towel or stick between you. Row in time: both lean forward, both pull back, counting "lean… pull… glide" — twenty strokes without dropping the rhythm. Then tug-of-water: gentle pulls against each other’s hold, feel the pull in the arms. In-time beats strong — that is the crew’s law.

Understanding check

Ask: "Name the three beats. Where does the power start? What must the whole crew share?" Lean-pull-glide, the legs, the rhythm — three answers and the boat flies.

Parent tips

Count EVERYTHING — the counting is the rhythm, and the rhythm is the skill. And keep pulls gentle in the towel game: this is rhythm training with strength sprinkled on top, not the other way round.

This lesson pairs with the Rowing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Canoeing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches canoeing’s quiet physics: dip on the left, dip on the right, and the boat goes straight — paddle one side only, and the boat spins. Steering, discovered by playing.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Canoeing is paddling an open boat with a single-bladed paddle, usually kneeling: dip, pull, switch sides, and the canoe glides ahead on calm water.

What does it mean?

The canoe is a physics lesson in disguise: every paddle stroke turns the boat a little, so going straight means SHARING the strokes between sides. One side only spins you in a circle — and four-year-olds adore proving it.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three canoeing ideas: the paddle dives on one side, pulls the water BACK, and lifts out — reach, pull, lift; strokes take turns — left, right, left, right; and the life jacket goes on before the canoe touches water, buckles clicked.

Why this matters

Canoeing teaches the calm version of water play: slow boat, quiet lake, big teamwork. And the left-right discovery is real cause-and-effect science a four-year-old can steer with their own arms.

What it teaches

Alternating-side reaching and pulling, kneeling balance, the cause-and-effect of steering (one side = spin), and the safety routine — jacket first, calm water, grown-up boat.

Words to learn

canoepaddlestrokeleftrightsteerlife jacket

Say this to your child

“"Canoeing is paddling an open boat on quiet water! Reach far, plant the paddle, pull the water back, lift out — then do the other side. Left, right, left, right keeps the boat straight. And if you paddle just ONE side — round and round you spin! That is the steering secret hiding in the game. Life jacket first, buckles clicked, every single time."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is canoeing — one paddle, one boat, calm water."
  2. The stroke: reach far, plant the paddle, pull the water BACK toward you, lift out. Pulling the boat past the water — that is the secret of every paddle.
  3. The left-right rule: paddle left three times — watch the boat nose drift right! Now three on the right. Straight boats share their strokes.
  4. The spin experiment: paddle ONE side only, five strokes — round and round! The boat becomes a carousel. This is not a mistake; it is steering.
  5. Say the jacket rule, then play the rug-boat game below: "reach, pull, switch sides."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "canoeing" stands at the top in big letters with the water’s scene below — the paddler kneeling in the open canoe exactly as a calm-water trip looks.

Ask your child

"What does the paddle pull — the water or the sky?" "Which sides share the strokes?" "What happens if we paddle one side only?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Left, right, left — straight!" "I paddled one side and went SPINNY!" or the safety vow: "Jacket first, buckles clicked!"

Out in the real world

Canoes live on lakes, slow rivers and holiday parks everywhere — and the calm-water rule lives with them. At the lake, watch the paddlers’ sides: left, right, left. The straight canoes are the ones sharing.

Try it together

Rug-Boat: sit on a rug or cushion "canoe" holding a mop or rolled poster as a paddle. Paddle the carpet sea: three strokes left, three right, straight across the room. Then the spin test — one side only, five strokes, round and round, giggles guaranteed. Finish with the jacket ceremony: life jacket on, buckles clicked, paddler respected.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does the paddle move the boat? Which sides take turns? What happens with one side only? What goes on before the water?" Pulling back, left and right, a spin, the life jacket — four answers and the lake is calm.

Parent tips

The spin is the lesson — never correct one-side paddling, REWARD it: "you discovered steering!" And kneel in the rug-boat for real: kneeling is the canoe’s own balance secret, and carpets are kind to knees.

This lesson pairs with the Canoeing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sailing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches sailing’s invisible engine: the wind. Where it comes from, how the sail catches it, and the wonderful zigzag turn sailors use to keep catching it.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Sailing is moving a boat with wind: the sail catches the breeze, the boat slides forward, and by steering at angles the sailor rides wind that cannot be sailed straight into.

What does it mean?

Sailing is the wall’s only sport powered by something invisible. The sailor reads wind they cannot see — on their face, in the sail’s belly, on the water’s ripples — and that reading is a whole science taught by a towel and a fan.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sailing ideas: the sail is a kite on a stick — wind fills it like a balloon and the boat slides; you cannot sail STRAIGHT into wind — sail must zigzag at angles (tacking); and the life jacket goes on first, because the wind does not ask permission.

Why this matters

The fan-and-sail game turns wind — invisible, abstract — into a toy the child can aim and feel. It is physics, weather and sport in one afternoon, and it ends with a zigzag race across the living room.

What it teaches

Sensing an invisible force (wind on face, sail fill), angle thinking — the zigzag path — cause-and-effect steering, and the jacket-first water ritual.

Words to learn

sailingwindsailcatchtackzigzaglife jacket

Say this to your child

“"Sailing has no engine and no paddles — the WIND is the engine! The sail catches it like a kite, and the boat slides across the water. But here is the secret: wind will not push a boat head-on. Sailors zigzag — one angle, then the other, tacking back and forth all the way to where they want to go. And life jacket first, always — the wind does not ask permission."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is sailing — the wind pushes, the boat glides."
  2. Feel the wind: blow on the back of the hand, fan the face — wind is moving air, and moving air PUSHES.
  3. The sail test: hold a towel or pillow up like a sail and walk — nothing. Now a partner FANS it — the sail fills, the "boat" wants to slide. Wind caught!
  4. The zigzag rule: try to walk straight INTO the fan — the sail flaps dead. Step sideways at an angle — full power! Sailors zigzag because wind only pushes from the side.
  5. Say the jacket rule, then play the fan-sail race below: "catch the wind, tack, glide."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "sailing" stands big at the top with the water’s scene below — the small boat and the full white sail exactly as a breeze-day on the bay looks.

Ask your child

"What pushes a sailing boat?" "Can we sail straight into the wind?" "What do sailors do instead?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The wind is the engine!" "I caught the wind in my sail!" or the sailor’s plan: "Zigzag — tack tack tack!"

Out in the real world

Sailing lives at every yacht club, harbour and breezy lake — and kids’ sailing courses start with exactly this: feel the wind, fill the sail, tack. On windy walks, find the flags and ripples together: the wind is writing its address all over the water.

Try it together

Fan-Sail Race: one player is the WIND with a paper fan; the other is the BOAT holding a towel-sail. The wind fan-blasts from different spots; the boat must keep the sail angled to catch it — never head-on! — and zigzag from sofa to sofa. Swap roles. The invisible force becomes a game piece, and tacking becomes the family’s new favourite word.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the engine of a sailboat? Why do sailors zigzag? What goes on first?" The wind, wind will not push head-on, the life jacket — three answers and the bay is open.

Parent tips

Let the head-on failure HAPPEN — the flapping dead sail is the moment the angle rule makes sense; no diagram teaches it faster. And on real water days, the jacket rule is said out loud every single time, without exceptions to negotiate.

This lesson pairs with the Sailing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Skating — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches skating where the ice is the hallway floor: the marching steps, the magical glide when the feet stop moving, and the soft fall every skater keeps in their pocket.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Skating is gliding on blades across ice: little marching steps first, then standing still while the ice carries you — the glide — then pushes and swoops and eventually spins, all on the shiniest, slipperiest floor there is.

What does it mean?

Skating flips walking’s rules: the floor MOVES. The skill is trusting the glide — feet still, body tall, momentum doing the work. Every skater remembers their first true glide the way other children remember their first bike.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three skating ideas: the march is small steps with toes turned slightly out; the glide is feet parallel, knees soft, NO stepping — let the ice (or floor) carry you; and falling is a SKILL: knees down, hands on knees, soft and giggly, always planned never feared.

Why this matters

Falling safely might be the most reusable skill in this whole class — skaters, judoka and playground kids all borrow it. And slipper-skating on the hallway floor builds the glide with zero cold, zero ice and zero bruises.

What it teaches

Dynamic balance on a low-friction surface, the stillness-while-moving glide, planned falling (a confidence skill as much as a safety one), and small-step bravery on new ground.

Words to learn

skatingiceglidemarchwobblefall softblades

Say this to your child

“"Skating is gliding on ice! Little marching steps first — toes out, wings out. Then the magic: stop stepping, knees soft, and LET THE ICE CARRY YOU. That glide is the best feeling in sport. And when we wobble — we fall SOFT: knees down, hands on knees, giggle, up again. Every skater falls; the good ones make friends with it."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is skating — gliding on the shiny ice."
  2. The march: little steps, toes out slightly, arms out like aeroplane wings. March a hallway lap.
  3. The glide: feet together-ish, knees soft, and STOP stepping — let the floor carry you. Count the glide: one… two… three! Every glide longer than the last.
  4. The soft fall: practise ON PURPOSE — sink to the knees, hands on knees, giggle. "Every skater falls; good skaters fall soft." Do it three times so it is a friend, not a fear.
  5. Play the slipper-rink game below and close: "march, glide, fall soft."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "skating" is printed large at the top with the rink’s scene below — the skater on shining blades exactly as a lap of the ice looks.

Ask your child

"What do our feet do first — march or glide?" "What do the knees do in a glide?" "What do we practise so falling is not scary?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I glided three whole counts!" "Wings out, toes out!" or the proud skater’s vow: "I fall soft — knees down, giggle!"

Out in the real world

Skating lives at every ice rink and winter festival — and in socks on every polished hallway floor. At the rink, hunt for glides: which skaters step-step-step forever, and which ones stand still and FLY?

Try it together

Slipper-Rink: socks on a smooth floor, the hallway is the rink. March the length, then glide — count it out loud. Add "hoops" (taped squares) to glide THROUGH, and the planned soft fall on a rug at the end, giggling. Helmet on if the floor is extra slippery — real rinks say yes to helmets for beginners, always.

Understanding check

Ask: "What comes first, march or glide? What do the knees do? What do we practise on purpose?" March, soft, the soft fall — three answers and the hallway is an ice rink.

Parent tips

Play glide contests, not speed races — stillness is the skill and counting the glide makes it visible. And do the deliberate soft fall until it is BORING: a fall that is boring is a fall that never scares.

This lesson pairs with the Skating flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Skiing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches skiing through its famous lunch menu: tips together for pizza (slow and stopped), tips apart for french fries (fast and free) — the two shapes every skier on Earth learns first.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Skiing is sliding down snow on long boards: legs bouncing like springs, tips together in a wedge (pizza!) to slow down, tips parallel (french fries!) to glide, poles trailing behind — the mountain does the pushing, the skier does the steering.

What does it mean?

Skiing inverts the usual rule: here the STOP is learned before the speed. The pizza wedge gives a four-year-old a brake they control with their own legs — which is why ski schools worldwide teach it before anything else.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three skiing ideas: pizza — ski tips together, heels out, the wedge that slows and stops; french fries — boards parallel, the glide that goes; and mountain knees are SOFT knees — the springs that drink every bump.

Why this matters

Named-after-lunch skills are unforgettable, and the wedge is safety and skill in one shape. Practised in socks down a carpet slope, it hands the child their brake before the mountain ever does.

What it teaches

Wedge braking from the hips, soft-knee absorption (springs, not sticks), edge awareness, and the mountain’s order of operations: stop first, speed second, always.

Words to learn

skiingsnowpizzafrench frieswedgeglideslope

Say this to your child

“"Skiing is sliding down the snow! Want to slow down? Tips together — PIZZA! The wedge stops the whole mountain. Want to glide? Boards straight — FRENCH FRIES! And your knees stay soft like springs the whole time, drinking every bump. Stop first, speed second — that is the mountain’s rule, and lunch names the moves."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is skiing — sliding down the mountain on long boards."
  2. Pizza: heels slide OUT, tips together — a thin wedge. Hold the shape. That is the brake.
  3. French fries: boards slide parallel — the glide. Say both shapes, be both shapes.
  4. Mountain knees: bounce gently — soft springs. Stiff legs bump, soft legs drink the bumps. Bounce-test everything.
  5. Play carpet-slope below and close: "pizza to stop, fries to go, springs all the way."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "skiing" leads at the top in big letters with the snow’s scene below — the skier on the snowy slope exactly as a green-run morning looks.

Ask your child

"Which shape slows us down?" "Which shape lets us glide?" "What are mountain knees — sticks or springs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Pizza! Tips together!" "Fries — I’m going fast!" or the mountain law: "Stop first, speed second!"

Out in the real world

Skiing owns the winter holidays of the US Rockies, the Canadian powder, the Australian and NZ snow fields — and every ski school on Earth teaches pizza first. On a snowy screen, hunt for the wedge: every beginner is a pizza; every racer is a fry.

Try it together

Carpet Slope: socks on, a smooth rug as the "run," the hallway the "mountain." Side-step UP the slope (skiers sidestep!), then slide down — fries for three counts, PIZZA to stop before the cushion-trees. Ten runs, alternating shapes. Then the bounce test: stiff legs vs spring legs over a bumpy towel — springs win, always.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which shape is the brake? Which shape is the glide? What do mountain knees drink?" Pizza, french fries, the bumps — three answers and the mountain is ready.

Parent tips

Practise the wedge STANDING STILL until the heels know the slide-out — then take it downhill. And keep the run short and the trees (cushions) far apart: early slopes are for shape-building, not courage-testing.

This lesson pairs with the Skiing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Curling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches curling’s friendly surprise: you slide the stone and then your TEAMMATES sweep the ice to steer it — the only sport where your throw keeps changing after your hand lets go.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Curling is a target game on ice: slide a big polished stone down the sheet toward a target of rings (the house), while teammates sweep the ice in front of it to make it go farther or curl less.

What does it mean?

Curling splits a throw into two jobs — the slider aims, the sweepers power. No other sport hands your throw to your friends mid-flight, which makes curling the gentlest team game on the wall.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three curling ideas: the stone is SLID, low and smooth, never thrown; the house is the target — rings to land in, closest to the middle wins; and sweeping melts a whisper of ice so the stone runs farther — sweeping is real, not pretend.

Why this matters

Kitchen-floor curling needs nothing but a lid and a paper plate, and the physics is real: smooth floor, sliding object, friction — the whole sport is a science experiment with a broom.

What it teaches

Underhand sliding with force control, target aiming, cooperative sweeping (helping a moving thing WITHOUT touching it), and turn order — curling is famously polite.

Words to learn

curlingstoneslidesweephousetargetice

Say this to your child

“"Curling is sliding a big smooth stone across the ice toward the rings — the house! Slide it LOW, never throw it. And here is the magic: your friends sweep the ice in front of the stone — sweep sweep sweep — and the sweeping makes it go FARTHER. You aim it, your friends steer it. The politest game on ice."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is curling — sliding the stone to the rings on the ice."
  2. The slide: crouch low, push the stone (a lid, a bean bag) along the floor with a smooth underhand slide — long and low, like feeding a cat under a fence. No throws!
  3. The house: paper plates in rings — middle is the button, landing near the middle wins.
  4. The sweep: two teammates fan or tea-towel the floor IN FRONT of the moving stone — never touching it. Watch: swept floors let stones run farther. Real physics!
  5. Play the kitchen curling game below and close: "slide low, aim middle, sweep sweep sweep."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "curling" stands big at the top with the rink’s scene below — the sliding stone and the target rings exactly as the game looks on the sheet.

Ask your child

"Do we throw the stone or slide it?" "What is the target called?" "What do the sweepers’ brushes do to the ice?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I slid it to the button!" "Sweep sweep — it went farther!" or the curler’s shout: "HURRY HARD!"

Out in the real world

Curling lives in Canada’s rinks and winter Olympics screens everywhere — and its soul lives on kitchen floors. Watch one end of a real game together: the slide, the sweepers, the polite nod. The politest athletes in the world.

Try it together

Kitchen Curling: paper-plate rings at one end of the smooth floor, plastic-lid stones, tea-towel brushes. Slide for the button — five stones each, closest wins the end. The sweeping rule: brushes may fan the floor in front of a moving stone, never touch it. Then try the spin: a little wrist twist makes the stone CURL — curve into the house like a proper curler.

Understanding check

Ask: "Slide or throw? What is the target called? What does sweeping do?" Slide, the house, makes it go farther — three answers and the kitchen is a rink.

Parent tips

Smooth floors only — rugs are the ice’s enemy. And let the sweepers truly matter: their fan-power genuinely carries stones farther, which turns teammates into co-throwers and keeps every player in the game.

This lesson pairs with the Curling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Skateboarding — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches skateboarding where it always starts: the stance on carpet — feet sideways, knees soft — because the strangest thing about a skateboard is that your body faces where the board is not going.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Skateboarding is riding a board on four small wheels: one foot forward near the front, push with the back foot, stand sideways, knees soft, and roll — flat ground first, ramps much later.

What does it mean?

Every other board on this wall points where you look. The skateboard stands you SIDEWAYS — and until the body accepts that, nothing else happens. The carpet stance solves the strangeness before the wheels exist.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three skateboarding ideas: the stance is sideways — front foot near the bolts, body facing the side; the push is gentle back-foot scoots, then that foot joins the board; and the gear rule is helmet AND pads before the board ever rolls.

Why this matters

The carpet-stance game removes skateboarding’s only scary part — facing sideways on wheels — and the helmet-and-pads ritual, worn from the first roll, is the habit that keeps skaters rolling for decades.

What it teaches

Side-on balance (new for every board game before it), single-foot pushing while the other balances, gear rituals, and the patience of flat ground before ramps.

Words to learn

skateboardstancesidewayspushrollhelmetpads

Say this to your child

“"Skateboarding is standing SIDEWAYS on a rolling board! Feet over the bolts, knees soft, arms out — the board goes forward but YOU face the side, and that is the fun of it. Little scoots with the back foot, then roll. And the rule that never bends: helmet buckled and pads on BEFORE the wheels move. Sideways, soft knees, gear on — then we roll."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is skateboarding — standing sideways on a rolling board."
  2. Carpet stance: board (or cushion) on carpet so it cannot roll. Feet SIDEWAYS over the bolts, knees soft, arms out. Hold five counts. Swap which foot leads — both are fine.
  3. The push: back foot off, little scoots along the carpet, foot back on. Scoot, scoot, ride.
  4. The gear ceremony: helmet on and buckled, pads on knees and elbows — the ritual that goes on BEFORE the wheels, every time, no exceptions.
  5. First roll (when ready): smooth flat pavement, gentle scoots, roll three metres, stamp the board still. Close with: "sideways, soft knees, gear on."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "skateboarding" is printed large at the top with the street’s scene below — the rider balanced on the wheeled board exactly as a first roll looks.

Ask your child

"Which way do our shoulders face — forward or sideways?" "Which foot pushes?" "What goes on before the wheels roll?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I stand sideways — the board faces forward!" "I pushed and rolled!" or the gear vow: "Helmet and pads first!"

Out in the real world

Skateboarding lives on every driveway, skatepark and school yard — and its Olympic debut made it official. Watch one park run together and find the soft knees: every smooth trick starts with bent springs, not stiff sticks.

Try it together

Carpet Stance School: board on carpet — sideways hold, soft knees, five counts, swap lead foot. Scoot laps along the carpet, push foot silent like a secret agent. Then the gear ceremony and (on a calm day) the first real three-metre roll on flat pavement, stamped to a stop. The stance was learned where nothing could roll — the street just receives it.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which way do we stand? What do the knees stay? What goes on before the wheels?" Sideways, soft, helmet and pads — three answers and the pavement is a playground.

Parent tips

Never skip the gear ceremony, not even for one push — the ritual IS the lesson, and rituals kept at four keep riders rolling at fourteen. And carpet first, always: a board that cannot roll lets the body learn the sideways truth safely.

This lesson pairs with the Skateboarding flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Climbing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches climbing as the thinking sport: the next hold is a question, the body answers with grip and reach, and the best climbers plan three moves before the first one.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Climbing is going UP a wall using hands and feet: grip the holds, push with the legs, reach for the next one — and always climb down as carefully as up. On playground ladders or real gym walls, the rules are the same.

What does it mean?

Climbing is cross-body thinking: right hand with left foot, reach across the middle, plan before moving. It builds grip strength, sequencing and the calm kind of bravery — and the descent is trained as hard as the climb.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three climbing ideas: the legs PUSH more than the arms pull — tired climbers find legs again; the reach crosses the body — right hand to a left-ish hold makes an X; and the rule of every wall: come down SLOW, three points touching when you can.

Why this matters

Grip strength and cross-lateral planning are two of the most borrowable skills on this wall — climbers grow into every racquet, bat and bar. And a child who plans three moves ahead has learned thinking-as-sport.

What it teaches

Grip strength and endurance, cross-lateral reaching, move sequencing (plan, then do), and the calm-down-skill — descending carefully is the deepest bravery in the lesson.

Words to learn

climbinggripreachholdplandownbrave

Say this to your child

“"Climbing is the thinking sport! Grip the hold like a jar lid, push with your strong legs, and reach ACROSS your body — right hand to the left-ish hold, an X! And before we climb, we PLAN: point at three holds, say their names, then go. And the rule that makes climbers brave: up slow, down SLOWER. Coming down is part of the climb."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is climbing — going up the wall with hands and feet planning together."
  2. The grip: fingers and thumbs wrap the hold like holding a big jar lid — whole hand, not just fingertips. Squeeze-test a doorway.
  3. The X-reach: practise on the floor first — right hand reaches up-LEFT, left foot steps — the body makes a letter X. Climbers are crossed.
  4. The plan: point at three holds and say them — red, blue, high one — THEN climb. Planning before moving is the sport’s brain.
  5. Play the tape-wall game below, and say the down rule: "up slow, down slower."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "climbing" leads at the top in big letters with the wall’s scene below — the climber on the colourful holds exactly as a gym wall looks from the mats.

Ask your child

"What pushes more — arms or legs?" "Which way does a climbing reach go — straight up or across in an X?" "What do we plan before we climb?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Legs are the strong ones!" "I planned three holds!" or the climber’s rule: "Up slow, down slower!"

Out in the real world

Climbing lives at every gym wall, playground ladder and climbing frame — and kids’ climbing courses teach exactly this: grip, X-reach, plan, down slow. On the playground, watch a climber’s feet: the strong ones push, they never dangle.

Try it together

Tape-Wall Climbing: paper "holds" taped at reaching heights on a smooth wall — feet stay on the floor. Touch the holds in planned order: call three, climb the pattern, hands only. Then the playground version: the ladder or frame with the three-point rule and the down-slower rule. Grip grows, the X grows, and the plan comes before every move.

Understanding check

Ask: "What pushes more? What letter does the reach make? What do we plan? And how do we come down?" The legs, an X, three holds, slower — four answers and the wall is friendly.

Parent tips

Feet-on-floor tape climbing is a real climbing workout — grip and reach grow without any height at all. And praise the careful DESCENT louder than the top-out: children who are celebrated for down-climbing stay safe on every wall they will ever meet.

This lesson pairs with the Climbing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Horse Riding — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches riding before any pony arrives: the tall seat, the soft hands, the walking-pace trot rhythm — so the first real ride feels like meeting a friend who already knows the rules.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Horse riding is riding with a large, kind animal: sit tall on the saddle, heels down, hold the reins gently, and ask with your seat and voice — walk, trot, whoa. The pony is a teammate, not a machine.

What does it mean?

Riding is the wall’s only partnership sport — half the team weighs half a tonne and has its own opinions. Children learn that calm voices, soft hands and patience move ponies; yanking and squeaking do not. It is manners with hooves.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three riding ideas: the seat is TALL — sit up like a flame on a candle, heels down; the hands are SOFT — hold the reins like holding a baby bird; and the helmet goes on FIRST, buckled, every ride, every pony, no exceptions.

Why this matters

Beyond the joy, riding teaches emotional regulation in a way no ball game can: the pony reads your body. A calm rider IS a safe rider — and that skill walks off the yard into the rest of life.

What it teaches

Posture and tall-seated balance, soft-grip hands (fine motor with a live partner), rhythm following in the rising trot, and the calm-body skill that ponies demand and reward.

Words to learn

horse ridingponysaddlereinshelmettrotcalm

Say this to your child

“"Horse riding is sitting tall on a pony teammate! Back straight like a flame on a candle, heels down, and hold the reins SOFT — like holding a baby bird. Your voice asks: walk on! And your seat says whoa. The pony listens to calm bodies. And the rule before everything, every ride: helmet on, buckled up. Tall seat, soft hands, helmet first."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is horse riding — sitting tall on a pony teammate."
  2. The seat: sit on a chair or cushion-horse — tall as a flame, shoulders back, HEELS DOWN. That is the rider’s shape.
  3. The soft hands: hold a rope or ribbon as reins — soft fists, arms elastic. Yank the rein? The pony’s mouth hurts. Soft hands all the way.
  4. The rising trot: up-down, up-down — stand and sit in rhythm while a partner counts or claps. That beat is the trot.
  5. The helmet ceremony: helmet ON, buckled, before any pony is mentioned. Then play the cushion-pony school below: "tall seat, soft hands, helmet first."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "horse riding" stand at the top in big letters with the yard’s scene below — the rider in a helmet on the pony exactly as a riding-school lesson looks.

Ask your child

"How do we sit — slumped or tall as a flame?" "How do hands hold the reins — tight or soft as a baby bird?" "What goes on our head first?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Heels down, sit tall!" "Soft hands — the pony likes gentle!" or the vow: "Helmet first, every ride!"

Out in the real world

Riding schools everywhere teach exactly this first: helmet, tall seat, soft hands, calm voice. Near a paddock, watch the riders’ hands — the ponies of soft-handed riders walk relaxed. The partnership is visible.

Try it together

Cushion-Pony School: a cushion on a chair is the pony. Mount from the "block" (step), find the tall seat, heels down, ribbon-reins in soft fists. The grown-up is the pony: walk, turn, halt — the rider asks with voice and seat, and the pony ONLY listens to soft hands and a calm voice. Rising trot to a clap rhythm. End with dismount and the helmet unbuckled — the ceremony closes like it opened.

Understanding check

Ask: "How does a rider sit? How do hands hold the reins? What comes first, every ride?" Tall as a flame, soft as a baby bird, the helmet — three answers and the yard is ready.

Parent tips

Never rush the real pony — the cushion school carries weeks of prep, and children who arrive knowing the seat and the soft hands are the ones riding schools remember fondly. And the helmet rule has no clever exceptions: it is said every lesson, out loud, first.

This lesson pairs with the Horse Riding flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Archery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches archery’s secret: the arrow goes where the CALM goes. The stance, the slow draw and the gentle release are all just calm — practised until it aims.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Archery is shooting arrows at a target with a bow: stand side-on, draw the string back slow, hold one quiet breath, and let go soft. The target’s middle — the gold — is the dream, but the routine is the skill.

What does it mean?

Every sport on this wall rewards speed somewhere. Archery is the one that rewards STILLNESS — the slow draw and the held breath are self-regulation dressed as sport, which is why calm children discover they were archers all along.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three archery ideas: the stance is side-on — feet apart, body facing the target’s edge; the draw is SLOW — string to the cheek, one breath held; and the release is a soft finger-open, never a fling. Plus the range rule, always: arrows up only when everyone is behind the line.

Why this matters

A suction-cup bow makes the sport safe, and the routine makes it teachable: stand, draw, breathe, release — a four-beat calm that children carry into every other waiting moment of their day.

What it teaches

Side-on stance, slow controlled pulling (draw strength is gentle strength), breath control and stillness, and the range discipline of lines and turn-taking — safety as a shared ritual.

Words to learn

archerybowarrowdrawaimreleasetarget

Say this to your child

“"Archery is the quiet game! Stand side-on, draw the string back slow — to your cheek, hold one breath — and let go SOFT with open fingers. The arrow flies where the calm goes. And the range rule that never bends: arrows up only when everyone is behind the line. Side-on, draw slow, let go soft — bullseye or not, the calm is the prize."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is archery — the quiet aiming game with a bow and arrow."
  2. The stance: side-on, feet apart, body facing the target’s shoulder — like a tennis serve’s sideways cousin.
  3. The draw: string back SLOW, hand to the cheek — the anchor. Hold one breath. The holding IS the aiming.
  4. The release: fingers open SOFT — the arrow is let go, never thrown. Practise the soft-open ten times with no arrow.
  5. Say the range rule, then play the target game below: "side-on, draw slow, let go soft."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "archery" stands large at the top with the range’s scene below — the bow, the arrow and the round target exactly as a shooting line looks.

Ask your child

"Which way do we stand — facing or side-on?" "Fast draw or slow draw?" "What does the release look like — a fling or a soft open?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Draw slow… hold… let go soft!" "My arrow flew straight!" or the range rule: "Arrows up when everyone’s behind the line!"

Out in the real world

Archery lives at clubs, camps and school sport days — suction-cup bows for beginners everywhere. On Olympic screens, watch one archer’s face at full draw: calm as a lake. That calm is the whole sport, visible.

Try it together

Paper-Plate Range: paper-plate target on a chair at one end of the room, suction-cup bow (or rubber-band cork-bow). The four-beat routine every shot: side-on… draw slow… one breath… soft open. Five arrows each, score the rings, praise the CALMEST shot loudest — not the closest. The range closes the same way it opened: arrows down, everyone behind the line.

Understanding check

Ask: "How do we stand? How do we draw? How do we let go? Who says when arrows can go up?" Side-on, slow, soft open, the range officer — four answers and the range is calm.

Parent tips

Praise routine over hits for the first month — a calm four-beat shot that misses teaches more than a fluke bullseye. And the line rule is a game, not a lecture: the "range officer" (rotating role) calls "arrows up!" — children love enforcing calm.

This lesson pairs with the Archery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Bowling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches bowling’s one golden rule — ROLL, never throw — and its quiet second life as the counting game: every fallen pin is a number shouted with joy.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Bowling is rolling a ball down a wooden lane to knock over ten white pins: one hand underneath, a smooth floor-level roll, and then the count — how many fell, how many stand?

What does it mean?

The underneath-roll is a genuine gross motor skill almost no other sport teaches — a push-along-the-ground that wants NO air time. And the scoring is the friendliest maths in sport: counting that everyone cheers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three bowling ideas: the ball ROLLS — one hand underneath, low and smooth along the floor, never thrown; the aim is the arrow marks or just the middle pin; and every roll ends in a count — fallen pins first, standing pins second.

Why this matters

Bowling is the perfect rainy-day card: a hallway, six bottles and any ball become a whole bowling alley — and the counting makes it a maths lesson wearing crash helmets.

What it teaches

Underhand ground-level rolling with force control, straight-line aiming, and the count — one-to-ten maths with crash sound effects built in.

Words to learn

bowlingrollpinslanestrikecountaim

Say this to your child

“"Bowling is the rolling game! One hand underneath, swing it back low, and ROLL it along the floor — never throw! Aim at the middle pin… roll… CRASH! Now count with me: how many fell down? How many still stand? Fallen plus standing makes ALL the pins — bowling is maths with crash sounds!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is bowling — rolling the ball at the pins."
  2. The roll: one hand UNDER the ball, swing it back low, let it roll OFF the fingers along the floor — like bowling it under a table. Practise the low swing five times, no ball.
  3. The aim: pick the middle pin and roll at IT — a small target makes straight rolls happen.
  4. The count: CRASH! — then count the fallen pins together, then the standing ones. Fallen plus standing should equal the whole set — that is the maths magic.
  5. Play the bottle-lane game below and close: "roll low, aim middle, count them all."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "bowling" leads at the top in big letters with the lane’s scene below — the rolling ball and the standing pins exactly as the approach looks.

Ask your child

"Do we throw or roll?" "Which pin do we aim at?" "What do we do after the crash?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Roll low — under the table!" "I knocked down five!" or the bowling maths: "Four fell, six stand — ten in all!"

Out in the real world

Bowling lives at every bowling alley and birthday party — bumper lanes and light balls exist exactly for small rollers. At the alley, watch the approach: good rollers stay LOW. The floor is the ball’s road, not the air’s.

Try it together

Bottle-Lane: six water bottles at the hallway’s end, any mid-size ball. Roll low from a tape line — five rolls each, count every crash, keep a shouting scoreboard. Then the maths magic: fallen plus standing always equals six. Rearrange the survivors into new shapes each round — triangles, towers — and roll again.

Understanding check

Ask: "Throw or roll? Which pin is the target? What do we shout while counting?" Roll, the middle pin, the numbers — three answers and the lane is open.

Parent tips

The under-the-table image fixes high throws instantly: "roll it like you’re bowling it under a table" works where "roll gently" never does. And keep the lane smooth and the pins forgiving — empty bottles fall beautifully and stand up again without tears.

This lesson pairs with the Bowling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fencing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches fencing’s real secret: it is a footwork sport wearing swords. The stance, the steps and the one big lunge carry the whole first lesson — the poking can wait a year.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Fencing is one-on-one sword play with masks and thin bending blades: en garde stance, advance and retreat on the feet, and touch the opponent’s jacket with the tip to score. It is chess at sprint speed, wrapped in extraordinary politeness.

What does it mean?

Fencing’s footwork is its treasure: side-on stance, quick small steps, balance held while moving fast — the same footwork boxers, tennis players and basketball defenders all borrow. The sword is almost a prop; the feet are the lesson.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fencing ideas: en garde — side-on, knees bent, sword up, mask on; the feet do the fighting — advance forward, retreat back, small quick steps; and the lunge is ONE big step with the front foot and a long arm — then straight back to en garde.

Why this matters

A pool-noodle duel makes the sport safe, and the etiquette makes it extraordinary: fencers salute before and shake hands after, every bout, forever. The manners are not decoration — they are the sport.

What it teaches

Side-on stance under movement, advance-retreat footwork (a rhythm skill), the lunge — one big coordinated step-and-reach — and the salute-and-handshake ritual.

Words to learn

fencingen gardeadvanceretreatlungemasksalute

Say this to your child

“"Fencing is the polite sword game! Mask on, en garde — side-on, knees springy, sword up. The feet do the fighting: advance… retreat… quick little steps. Then ONE big lunge — step and reach, touch the target — and back to en garde. And before every bout we salute, and after we shake hands. Fencers are the politest sword-fighters in the world."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is fencing — the sword game with masks and manners."
  2. En garde: side-on, feet in a comfortable L, knees bent, noodle-sword UP, mask (or helmet-pretend) on. Hold the stance — it should feel springy.
  3. The footwork: ADVANCE — front foot steps, back foot follows. RETREAT — back foot steps, front follows. Small quick steps, up the hallway and back.
  4. The lunge: front foot BIG step, arm reaches long — touch the cushion-target — then straight back to en garde. One lunge is one whole firework.
  5. Play the noodle duel below and close with the salute: "en garde, advance, LUNGE — and always salute."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "fencing" stands at the top in big letters with the strip’s scene below — two masked fencers and their crossed thin swords exactly as a bout looks.

Ask your child

"What do the feet do — big stomps or quick small steps?" "What is the one big step called?" "What do fencers do before and after every bout?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "En garde!" "Advance, advance, LUNGE!" or the fencer’s manners: "We salute first — and shake hands after!"

Out in the real world

Fencing lives at clubs and school gyms — and on Olympic screens where the footwork is easiest to see. Watch one bout together and ignore the swords entirely: watch the FEET. Quick small steps, always springy.

Try it together

Noodle Duel: two pool-noodle swords, cushion-target between the fencers. Round one: footwork only — advance and retreat, mirror each other, no touching. Round two: one lunge each at the cushion, back to en garde. Round three: the mask-on duel — gentle noodle touches on the sword or target only, never people — then the salute and the handshake. Salute first, shake after: the ritual IS the sport.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the stance called? What do the feet do? What is the one big step? What happens before and after?" En garde, advance and retreat, the lunge, the salute — four answers and the strip is open.

Parent tips

Footwork rounds outnumber duelling rounds three to one — the feet are the curriculum. And noodle touches land on swords and targets ONLY; the rule is stated before round one and honoured by the grown-up’s own noodle first.

This lesson pairs with the Fencing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Boxing — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches boxing the way good gyms do: stance and guard first, straight punches at PADS only, and the rule spoken out loud in every round — pads and bags, never people.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Boxing is the punch sport with big gloves: guard up protecting the face, feet springy, straight jabs and crosses at pads, bags and nothing else. Real boxers are among the fittest athletes alive.

What does it mean?

For little ones, boxing is pad-work fitness: a strong stance, fast straight arms, bouncing feet — and the discipline of WHERE punching is allowed. The rule is not a warning on the side of the lesson; the rule is the lesson.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three boxing ideas: the guard — fists up by the cheeks, elbows in, protecting the face; the jab is STRAIGHT — out and back down the same road, fast; and the rule — pads, bags and cushions are the only targets, ever, in every round.

Why this matters

Pad rounds are pure joy — thirty seconds of jab-jab-cross with a roaring finish — and they build the strongest shoulders and straightest punches on this wall, inside the safest rule in sport.

What it teaches

Straight punching mechanics (out-and-back on one road), guard posture, springy footwork, thirty-second effort bursts, and rule-keeping under excitement — the deepest skill in the gym.

Words to learn

boxingguardjabcrosspadsroundstraight

Say this to your child

“"Boxing is the pad-punching sport! Fists up by your cheeks — that is the guard. Jab — straight out, straight back, one road. Jab, jab, CROSS! But here is the rule, and it never changes: we punch PADS and BAGS, never people, never pets, never walls. Boxers are the fittest, politest punchers in the world — the rule is why."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is boxing — the pad-punching fitness sport."
  2. The guard: fists up by the cheeks, elbows tucked, chin soft. Say the rule BEFORE the first punch: "pads and bags, never people."
  3. The jab: straight out from the cheek, straight back to the cheek — one road, out and home. Ten quiet jabs in the air.
  4. The cross: the other hand’s straight punch with a small hip turn — jab-jab-CROSS is the drumbeat.
  5. Play the pad rounds below and end every round with the rule, out loud: "pads and bags, never people."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "boxing" leads at the top in big letters with the gym’s scene below — the gloves and the training pads exactly as a pad-round looks.

Ask your child

"Where do the fists live in the guard? What road does the jab travel? What are the ONLY targets in boxing?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Guard up — fists by my cheeks!" "Jab, jab, CROSS!" or the rule, unprompted: "Pads and bags, never people!"

Out in the real world

Boxing gyms everywhere welcome kids’ pad-work classes — and every one of them teaches the same rule first. On screen, watch one pad round: the trainer’s pads are the only things the gloves ever touch. That is boxing’s own discipline, visible.

Try it together

Pad Rounds: grown-up holds cushions as pads. Round one: thirty seconds of jab-jab-cross, feet bouncing, big finish cheer. Round two: jab on the MOVE — follow the pads around the room. Round three: child’s choice, but the round must END with the rule said out loud. Three rounds, water break, guard-up parade lap. Fitness, straightness, and a rule kept with pride.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the guard? What road does the jab take? What are the only targets?" Fists by the cheeks, out-and-back straight, pads and bags — three answers and the round is on.

Parent tips

Hold the pads LOW for little arms — shoulder height is grown-up height. And if any punch ever drifts toward a person, the round pauses instantly and calmly: the rule is the lesson, and pausing proves it — warmly, every time.

This lesson pairs with the Boxing flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Judo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches judo’s two first skills — the gentle grip and the soft fall — because judo literally means "the gentle way," and its best gift to a four-year-old is knowing how to fall without hurt, for life.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Judo is a mat art from Japan: partners in white suits grip each other’s jackets, step, balance and unbalance — and the most practised skill of all is falling SAFELY, slapping the mat like a starfish.

What does it mean?

Judo flips the fear: every beginner learns to FALL before learning to throw. The break-fall turns the scariest part of moving into a party trick — and it transfers to skating rinks, skateboards and slippery floors forever.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three judo ideas: the bow comes first — respect to the partner and the mat, every session; the grip is gentle — sleeve and elbow, holding a friend, not a rope; and the break-fall is the starfish — roll back, arms slap wide, soft and loud.

Why this matters

"The gentle way" is the whole philosophy in two words: maximum effect with minimum effort, respect before everything. For four-year-olds, judo is manners, balance and safe falling in white pyjamas.

What it teaches

Safe falling (the break-fall is a lifelong injury-prevention skill), gentle-grip partner work, static and moving balance, and the respect ritual — bow first, always.

Words to learn

judogentlegripbalancebreak-fallmatbow

Say this to your child

“"Judo means the gentle way! We bow first — to our partner and the mat. We grip the jacket soft — sleeve and elbow, like holding a friend. We step and balance like tall trees. And the best trick in judo is falling SOFTLY — roll back, arms out wide, SLAP the mat like a starfish. Everyone falls; judoka are the ones who fall well."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is judo — the gentle way on the mats."
  2. The bow: hands slide to the knees, small bow to the partner. Every judo session starts here — respect first, always.
  3. The grip: hold a partner’s sleeve and elbow (or their jacket shoulders) — firm as holding a friend’s hand, gentle as holding a bird.
  4. The break-fall: sit on a mat or bed, roll back one small roll, arms SLAP wide like a starfish — slap! Loud and soft at once. Three falls, giggling.
  5. Play the balance games below and close with the bow: "grip gentle, fall soft, bow first."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "judo" stands big at the top with the mat’s scene below — two partners in white suits gripping jackets exactly as a randori looks.

Ask your child

"What does judo mean?" "What comes first, every session?" "How do judoka fall — hard or soft like a starfish?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The gentle way!" "I gripped the sleeve soft!" or the proudest one: "SLAP — I break-fell like a starfish!"

Out in the real world

Judo lives in clubs across Japan, France, Brazil and every Olympic Games — and its break-fall lives in every swim school’s safety roll and every skateboarder’s first tumble. The gentle way is everywhere once you can see it.

Try it together

Starfish Fall School: on a bed or mat — sit, roll back, arms SLAP wide, giggle, repeat. Then the jacket-grip walk: partners grip sleeve-and-elbow and walk a slow circle, one leading, one following, roles swapped on a clap. Finish with tall-tree balance: one foot, arms wide, three counts — and the closing bow. Gentle, every step.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does judo mean? What do we do first, every session? How do we fall?" The gentle way, the bow, soft like a starfish — three answers and the mat is a friend.

Parent tips

Make the fall the STAR, not the throw — four-year-olds who can break-fall beautifully are ready for everything else at their own pace. And never skip the bow: it costs three seconds and carries the whole philosophy.

This lesson pairs with the Judo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Karate — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches karate as the manners programme wearing a punch: the bow, the counted kata, the blocks before punches — and the control of stopping every punch in the air.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Karate means "empty hand" — a Japanese art of blocks, punches and kicks done with no weapons: strong low blocks, straight punches that STOP in the air, and kata — patterns of moves counted out loud.

What does it mean?

The hidden curriculum of karate is control: every punch stops short, every partner is bowed to, every class starts and ends with respect. Children learn that power and manners arrive together or not at all.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three karate ideas: the bow opens and closes everything; blocks come BEFORE punches — low, middle, high; and the punch is straight and STOPPED — air control proves the discipline.

Why this matters

The counted kata — ichi, ni, san, shi — is focus training disguised as a drill: four moves in order, in Japanese, with a big voice. It is the wall’s best first lesson in doing things IN ORDER.

What it teaches

Sequencing (the kata is an ordered plan), blocking mechanics, air-stopping control (punch power with a brake), and the counting itself — Japanese one-to-four is a genuine first foreign-language souvenir.

Words to learn

karateempty handblockpunchkatabowichi ni san shi

Say this to your child

“"Karate means empty hand — no weapons, just your body! We bow first: oss! Blocks come before punches: low, middle, high. Then the straight punch — out from the hip and STOP in the air, because karate power comes with karate control. And we count in Japanese: ichi, ni, san, shi! Bow. Oss!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is karate — empty hand, strong blocks, straight punches."
  2. The bow: fists to the palm, small bow — oss! Every kata begins and ends here.
  3. The three blocks: LOW (arms cross down), MIDDLE (forearm across the tummy), HIGH (forearm over the head). Blocks before punches — say it, mean it.
  4. The stopped punch: straight out from the hip, STOP in the air — no partner, no target, full control. Control IS the skill.
  5. Teach the kata below and close with the bow: "block, block, block, punch — ichi ni san shi!"

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "karate" is printed large at the top with the dojo’s scene below — the child in the white suit mid-move exactly as a first kata looks.

Ask your child

"What does karate mean? What comes before punches? Where does the punch stop? What are the counting words?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Empty hand!" "Low, middle, high — blocks first!" or the counted kata: "Ichi, ni, san, SHI!"

Out in the real world

Karate lives in dojos on every street corner of the four countries this class calls home — the white suits and coloured belts are the world’s most visible children’s sport. Watch one kids’ class: the bowing is not decoration, it is half the lesson.

Try it together

The First Kata: bow, then four moves down an imaginary line — low block (ichi), middle block (ni), high block (san), straight stopped punch (shi) — counted in a BIG voice. Turn, repeat the other way. Three lines make a whole kata: bow, and oss! Belt ceremony: any coloured ribbon tied on, one thing praised about the manners, not the punches.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does karate mean? What comes before punches? What does the punch do in the air? Count the kata." Empty hand, blocks, stops, ichi-ni-san-shi — four answers and the dojo is open.

Parent tips

The air-stop is the discipline engine — a punch that can stop can be trusted, and children feel that trust immediately. And count in Japanese every single time: four words of a second language, worn like a belt.

This lesson pairs with the Karate flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Taekwondo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches taekwondo, the kicking art of Korea: springy feet, one-leg balance, front kick and roundhouse at pads only — the wall’s best one-leg balance training wearing a black belt.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Taekwondo is Korea’s martial art, famous for kicks: front kicks, side kicks and the spinning roundhouse, all drilled at pads and targets. Fast feet, flexible legs, and balance that holds on one leg while the other one works.

What does it mean?

Kicking is the wall’s finest one-leg balance challenge: the kicking leg swings while the standing leg owns the ground. Taekwondo trains that split — work and stand — a hundred times a class, which is why taekwondo kids hop like herons.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three taekwondo ideas: the stance is springy — feet apart, knees soft, hands up; the front kick is knee UP, foot OUT, foot BACK — a snap, not a stomp; and every kick lands on a PAD held by the grown-up — pads, never people, same rule as boxing’s.

Why this matters

One-leg balance is the quiet king of this whole class — every skater, batter and kicker borrows it — and taekwondo drills it with more joy per minute than anything else on the wall.

What it teaches

Single-leg dynamic balance, hip flexibility (the knee-up is a real stretch), kicking mechanics in snaps, and the pad-only discipline shared by every striking art.

Words to learn

taekwondoKoreakickfront kickroundhousepadbalance

Say this to your child

“"Taekwondo is the kicking sport from Korea! Springy stance, knees soft — then the front kick: knee UP, foot snaps OUT, foot comes BACK. Snap! And the roundhouse swings round like a door. Every kick lands on a PAD the grown-up holds — pads, never people. Ten kicks each leg, counting loud — and your standing leg learns to be a tree while the other one flies."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is taekwondo — the kicking art from Korea."
  2. The stance: feet apart, knees soft, fists up — springy like a kangaroo waiting for a joke.
  3. The front kick: knee UP high first, foot snaps OUT, foot comes BACK down — knee, out, back. Practise in slow motion five times, then fast.
  4. The roundhouse: same knee-up, but the foot swings ROUND sideways — a door swinging on the hip hinge. Slow-motion first, always.
  5. Play the pad-kick drill below and close: "knee up, snap out, pads only."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "taekwondo" stands at the top in big letters with the dojang’s scene below — the high kick toward the pad exactly as a kicking drill looks.

Ask your child

"Which country’s art is taekwondo? What comes up first — the foot or the knee? What do kicks land on?"

What your child can say or do
