Your child might say: "Knee up, snap out!" "My roundhouse went THWACK!" or the pad rule: "Kicks on pads, never people!"

Out in the real world

Taekwondo is an Olympic sport and a school-club staple across the US, Canada, Australia and NZ — the belts and the pad-thwacks are everywhere. Watch one kids’ class: the heron-leg balance is the quiet skill behind every loud kick.

Try it together

Pad-Kick Drill: a cushion held at knee height by the grown-up — front kick, kick, kick, ten each leg, counted loud. Then the roundhouse cushion, swung gently sideways — five each side. Balance challenge to finish: standing-leg tree pose while the other foot "kicks the air" three slow times. Wobbles are the training; the pad is the target; the counting is the music.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the kick start? What order — knee, out, back? What do kicks land on?" The knee, knee-out-back, pads — three answers and the dojang is springy.

Parent tips

Slow-motion kicks first — the knee-up order is the whole technique, and speed arrives on its own. And swap which leg kicks first: both legs deserve to learn, and balance grows twice as fast.

This lesson pairs with the Taekwondo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · SPORTS & MOVEMENT · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Weightlifting — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches weightlifting’s real gift: not the overhead press but the pattern underneath it — bend the KNEES, keep the back straight, hold it close — the safe-lifting rule every human body uses forever.

Download the card ↓

How to use this card

What is this?

Weightlifting is the Olympic strength sport: lifters pull a heavy barbell from the floor and press it clean overhead in one strong, precise moment — legs drive, back stays straight, the lift is speed and shape, not just muscle.

What does it mean?

Under the chalk and the roar, weightlifting teaches the exact lifting pattern school bags and grocery bags will demand for a lifetime: knees bend, back straight, load close. Four is the perfect age to build the habit with a noodle.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three weightlifting ideas: the lift starts with BENT KNEES and a straight back — never a bent-back pull; the load stays CLOSE to the body; and everything comes DOWN slow — lifting is half the lift, lowering is the other half.

Why this matters

The pool-noodle barbell makes the sport safe and silly, and the pattern it drills — knees, back, close, slow — is the single most reusable skill in this whole class: it walks out of the living room and into every heavy bag a child will ever carry.

What it teaches

The safe-lifting pattern (hip hinge with knee bend — a lifetime injury-prevention skill), overhead press with a braced middle, slow eccentric lowering, and lift-and-cheer effort cycles.

Words to learn

weightliftingbarbellliftkneesstraight backpressstrong

Say this to your child

“"Weightlifting is the strong sport! Feet apart, knees BENT, back straight as a plank — hold the barbell close to your buttons. Now push the floor away, stand tall, and PRESS it overhead — UP! Hold it like a trophy… and lower it DOWN slow, slow, slow. Strong lifters bend their knees, not their backs — and that is also how you lift your school bag forever."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is weightlifting — the strong sport of lifting things well."
  2. The setup: feet apart, noodle-barbell (or broom) in wide hands, knees BENT, back STRAIGHT, chest proud. That shape is the lift’s foundation.
  3. The lift: push the floor away with the legs, stand tall, barbell stays CLOSE to the body — grazing the shirt buttons.
  4. The press: strong arms push it UP overhead — body tall, tummy braced — hold two counts, then lower it DOWN slow, slow, slow.
  5. Play the soft-barbell lift below and close: "knees bend, back straight, down slow."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "weightlifting" stands big at the top with the platform’s scene below — the barbell lifted strong overhead exactly as a clean-and-jerk looks.

Ask your child

"What bends — the knees or the back? Where does the barbell stay on the way up? What happens slow — the lift or the lower?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Knees bent, back straight!" "I pressed it UP like a trophy!" or the lifter’s law: "Down slow — lowering is half the lift!"

Out in the real world

Weightlifting is the oldest Olympic strength sport — and its knee-bend rule lives in every school bag, grocery bag and pet-cat pickup in the world. Next heavy carry, do it out loud together: knees bend, back straight, hold it close.

Try it together

Soft-Barbell Club: pool noodle with two socks as plates. Five lifts with the pattern chanted every rep: "knees bend… back straight… hold close… UP… down slow." Then the grocery relay: carry soft items one at a time from the "store" (sofa) to the "kitchen" (chair) with perfect lifting form — the bag-lift pattern, practised as a game. Finish with a strong-lifter flex and a chalk-drawn medal.

Understanding check

Ask: "What bends, what stays straight? Where does the barbell travel? Which half is slow?" The knees, back straight, close to the body, the lower — four answers and the club is strong.

Parent tips

Chant the pattern on every rep — the words carry the shape, and the shape becomes automatic. And never add real weight: the noodle IS the programme; the pattern is the prize that lasts a lifetime.

This lesson pairs with the Weightlifting flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Sports & Movement (Class 37).
